biology-paper-1.title: Cell Structure and Microscopy
biology-paper-1.description: Covers eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells (4.1.1.1), animal and plant cells (4.1.1.2), cell special...
biology-paper-1.content_html:
Eukaryotic and Prokaryotic Cells

All living things are made of cells. Cells are divided into two fundamental types: eukaryotic cells and prokaryotic cells. Understanding the differences between these two types is a core part of AQA and is regularly tested in exams.

Eukaryotic cells include both animal and plant cells. They have a nucleus that encloses their genetic material (DNA), along with other membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells — bacteria — are much smaller and simpler. They lack a true nucleus: instead, their genetic material is a single loop of DNA that floats freely in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes may also contain small rings of extra DNA called plasmids.

Key Fact

Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus that encloses their DNA. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus — their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and they may also contain plasmids.

A typical animal cell is around 10–30 µm (micrometres) in diameter. A prokaryotic bacterial cell is much smaller, typically 1–5 µm. You need to be comfortable converting between units and using standard form. The key prefixes are: centi (\(10^{-2}\)), milli (\(10^{-3}\)), micro (\(10^{-6}\)) and nano (\(10^{-9}\)).

Animal and Plant Cells

Both animal and plant cells are eukaryotic, but they contain different organelles. You must be able to name each organelle and explain how its structure relates to its function.

Nucleus — contains the cell’s genetic material (DNA) and controls the cell’s activities. The DNA carries the instructions for making proteins.

Cytoplasm — a jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions take place. Enzymes in the cytoplasm control these metabolic reactions.

Cell membrane — a thin layer that surrounds the cell and controls which substances enter and leave. It is selectively permeable.

Mitochondria — the site of aerobic respiration, where energy is transferred from glucose. Cells that need lots of energy (such as muscle cells) contain more mitochondria.

Ribosomes — tiny structures in the cytoplasm where protein synthesis occurs. They are found in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

Plant cells have all of the organelles listed above, plus three additional structures:

Chloroplasts — contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. They absorb light energy to make glucose.

Permanent vacuole — a large, fluid-filled space containing cell sap (a weak solution of sugars and salts). It helps keep the cell rigid and supports the plant.

Cell wall — made of cellulose and surrounds the cell membrane. It strengthens and supports the cell, preventing it from bursting when water enters by osmosis.

Key Fact

Plant cells have a cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a permanent vacuole (cell sap) in addition to the organelles found in animal cells. Bacterial cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, no true nucleus and no mitochondria.

Cell Specialisation

Not every cell in an organism looks the same. Cells become specialised — they develop particular structures that allow them to perform a specific function. The exam regularly asks you to explain how a cell’s structure relates to its function.

Sperm cell — has a streamlined head, a long tail (flagellum) for swimming, and many mitochondria to provide energy for movement. It carries the male DNA to the egg.

Nerve cell (neurone) — has a long axon to carry electrical impulses over long distances, branched endings (dendrites) to connect with other nerve cells, and a myelin sheath to insulate the signal and speed up transmission.

Muscle cell — contains many mitochondria to supply energy for contraction. Muscle cells are elongated so they can contract and relax to produce movement.

Red blood cell — has a biconcave disc shape to increase surface area for absorbing oxygen. It has no nucleus, leaving more room to carry haemoglobin.

Root hair cell — has a long, thin extension (the root hair) that increases the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil by osmosis and active transport.

Xylem cell — a hollow, dead tube reinforced with lignin that transports water and mineral ions from roots to leaves in a continuous column. The hollow centre (lumen) allows uninterrupted flow.

Phloem cell — has sieve plates with tiny pores that allow dissolved sugars to flow through the plant from leaves to other parts. This movement is called translocation.

Cell Differentiation

The process by which a cell becomes specialised is called differentiation. As a cell differentiates, it acquires the sub-cellular structures it needs for its function.

Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage of development — during embryonic growth. Once they have specialised, they generally cannot change into a different cell type, and cell division in mature animals is mainly for repair and replacement. Plant cells, however, retain the ability to differentiate throughout their lives. Undifferentiated plant cells are found in regions called meristems, located at the tips of roots and shoots. This is why you can take a cutting from a plant and it will grow into a new individual.

Key Fact

Most animal cells differentiate early in development and are then permanently specialised. Plant cells can differentiate throughout life because they retain meristem tissue — undifferentiated cells at root and shoot tips.

Microscopy

Microscopes allow us to see cells and sub-cellular structures that are invisible to the naked eye. There are two main types you need to know: light microscopes and electron microscopes.

Light microscopes use glass lenses and visible light to produce a magnified image. They have a maximum useful magnification of about \(\times 1{,}500\) and a resolution of around 200 nm. Light microscopes were first developed in the 1590s and allowed scientists to discover cells for the first time.

Electron microscopes fire a beam of electrons at the specimen rather than using light. They have a much higher resolution (down to about 0.2 nm) and a useful magnification of up to \(\times 2{,}000{,}000\). This allows biologists to see sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and the internal structure of mitochondria in much finer detail. The development of electron microscopes in the 1930s was a turning point — it revealed structures inside cells that no one had seen before.

Key Fact

Light microscopes: max magnification \(\approx \times 1{,}500\), resolution \(\approx 200\) nm. Electron microscopes: max magnification \(\approx \times 2{,}000{,}000\), resolution \(\approx 0.2\) nm. Higher resolution means finer detail can be distinguished.

You must be able to use and rearrange the magnification formula:

$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{size of image}}{\text{size of real object}}$$

This can be rearranged to find the real size or the image size:

$$\text{real size} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}}$$

$$\text{image size} = \text{magnification} \times \text{real size}$$

Worked example: A student measures the image of a cell as 30 mm across. The real cell is 0.03 mm (30 µm). Calculate the magnification.

$$\text{magnification} = \frac{30}{0.03} = \times 1{,}000$$

Always check both measurements are in the same units before dividing. Express very large or very small answers in standard form where appropriate.

Required Practical 1: Using a Light Microscope

AQA Required Practical 1 asks you to use a light microscope to observe, draw and label plant and animal cells. You could be examined on the method, results, and how to calculate magnification from a drawing. Here is the standard procedure:

Step 1: Place a thin specimen (e.g. a layer of onion epidermis or a cheek cell smear) on a clean glass slide.

Step 2: Add a drop of water (for plant cells) or a stain such as iodine (to make structures more visible). Methylene blue is used for animal cells.

Step 3: Lower a coverslip at an angle using a mounted needle to avoid trapping air bubbles, which distort the image.

Step 4: Clip the slide onto the microscope stage and select the lowest power objective lens first.

Step 5: Use the coarse focus knob to bring the image roughly into focus, then the fine focus knob to sharpen it.

Step 6: To see more detail, switch to a higher power objective lens and refocus using the fine adjustment only.

Drawing rules: Use a sharp pencil. Draw clear, continuous lines (no shading). Label key structures with straight ruled lines. Include a title, the magnification used, and a scale bar.

Key Fact

Required Practical 1: Always start on the lowest power objective, use a stain to make structures visible, lower the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, and include a magnification scale on your biological drawing.

When answering questions on cell structure, always link the organelle to its function — for example, “mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which transfers energy for the cell.” In magnification calculations, the most common mistake is forgetting to convert units so that both image size and real size are in the same unit (usually mm or µm) before dividing. Always show every step of your working — you can pick up method marks even if the final answer is wrong. For Required Practical 1, be ready to describe the method and explain why each step matters (e.g. “the coverslip is lowered at an angle to prevent air bubbles, which would distort the image”).

Key Takeaways

  • Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus and may contain plasmids.
  • Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole in addition to the organelles found in animal cells.
  • Cells specialise through differentiation — most animal cells differentiate early, but plant cells can differentiate throughout life via meristems.
  • Electron microscopes have far higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes, enabling scientists to see sub-cellular detail.
  • The magnification formula is \(\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{real size}}\) — always convert to the same units first.

biology-paper-1.title: Cell Division and Transport
biology-paper-1.description: How cells divide by mitosis and meiosis, plus osmosis, diffusion and active transport.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

Cells in your body divide to grow, repair damaged tissue and replace worn-out cells. This process follows a pattern called the cell cycle. Most of the cell cycle is spent in a growth phase called interphase, during which the cell’s DNA is replicated and the number of sub-cellular structures (organelles) increases.

Once the cell has copied all of its DNA and organelles, it enters mitosis. During mitosis, one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell. The cytoplasm and cell membrane then divide to produce two genetically identical daughter cells. Each daughter cell has the full set of 46 chromosomes (in humans).

Key Fact

Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell. It is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. The cell cycle consists of interphase (growth + DNA replication) followed by mitosis and cell division.

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and become specialised. In humans, embryonic stem cells can differentiate into almost any cell type, while adult stem cells (found in bone marrow) are more limited. In plants, meristem tissue retains the ability to differentiate throughout the plant’s life.

Stem cells have therapeutic uses — for example, treating paralysis or diabetes — but raise ethical concerns, particularly around the use of embryonic stem cells. You need to be able to discuss both the potential benefits and the ethical objections.

Diffusion

Diffusion is the spreading out of particles from a region where they are at a higher concentration to a region where they are at a lower concentration. It occurs in both liquids and gases and does not require energy. Oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out of cells by diffusion.

The rate of diffusion is affected by the concentration gradient (a steeper gradient means faster diffusion), the temperature (higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy), the surface area of the membrane and the distance the particles must travel.

Key Fact

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration. It is a passive process (no energy required). Factors affecting rate: concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and distance.

Osmosis

Osmosis is the movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution (high water concentration) to a more concentrated solution (low water concentration). Like diffusion, osmosis is a passive process.

In Required Practical 3, you investigate the effect of a range of sugar solutions on the mass of plant tissue. Potato cylinders placed in distilled water gain mass (water enters cells by osmosis) while those in concentrated sugar solution lose mass (water leaves cells).

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration. This requires energy from cellular respiration. Examples include root hair cells absorbing mineral ions from the soil and the absorption of sugar from the gut into the blood.

Active transport is essential when a cell needs to accumulate substances at a higher concentration than the surrounding environment. The energy for this process comes from the mitochondria.

Comparing Transport Methods

A common exam question asks you to compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport. Diffusion and osmosis are passive (no energy needed) and move substances down the concentration gradient. Active transport requires energy and moves substances against the concentration gradient. Osmosis specifically describes the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.

biology-paper-1.title: Organisation and the Digestive System
biology-paper-1.description: From cells to organ systems, with a focus on how the digestive system breaks down food.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
Levels of Organisation

The human body is organised into a hierarchy. Individual cells with a similar structure and function are grouped together into tissues. Different tissues combine to form organs, and organs work together as organ systems. The digestive system is one of the main organ systems you need to know.

Key Fact

The hierarchy of organisation: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism. Each level builds on the one below it.

The Digestive System

The digestive system is a muscular tube running from the mouth to the anus. Its role is to break large, insoluble food molecules into smaller, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood. Digestion involves both mechanical breakdown (teeth, churning in the stomach) and chemical breakdown by enzymes.

The main digestive enzymes are:

  • Amylase — produced in the salivary glands and pancreas; breaks down starch into sugars (maltose).
  • Proteases — produced in the stomach (pepsin), pancreas and small intestine; break down proteins into amino acids.
  • Lipases — produced in the pancreas and small intestine; break down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.

Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is released into the small intestine where it has two key functions: it neutralises the hydrochloric acid from the stomach (creating alkaline conditions for enzymes in the small intestine) and it emulsifies fats — breaking large fat droplets into smaller ones to increase the surface area for lipase to work on.

Key Fact

Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and emulsifies fats in the small intestine. It also neutralises stomach acid to create the alkaline conditions needed by intestinal enzymes.

Enzymes and the Lock-and-Key Model

Enzymes are biological catalysts — they speed up reactions without being used up. Each enzyme has a specific active site with a unique shape. Only a substrate with the matching shape can fit into the active site, like a key in a lock. This is called the lock-and-key model.

Enzymes work best at an optimum temperature and pH. If the temperature is too high or the pH is too extreme, the active site changes shape (denaturation) and the substrate can no longer fit. The enzyme stops working.

You should know the food tests for AQA Required Practical 2:

  • Starch — Iodine solution turns from brown-orange to blue-black.
  • Sugars — Benedict’s reagent heated; turns from blue to green/yellow/orange/red (depending on sugar concentration).
  • Proteins — Biuret reagent turns from blue to purple/lilac.
  • Lipids — Sudan III test; a red layer forms if lipids are present.

The digestive system demonstrates how organs work together as a system. The stomach churns food and adds acid; the pancreas produces enzymes; the liver makes bile; the small intestine absorbs soluble products into the blood; and the large intestine absorbs water.

biology-paper-1.title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease
biology-paper-1.description: The structure of the heart, blood vessels and blood, plus coronary heart disease treatments.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
The Heart

The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood around the body through a double circulatory system. The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circuit). The left side pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body (systemic circuit).

The heart has four chambers: two upper atria (singular: atrium) that receive blood, and two lower ventricles that pump blood out. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right because it needs to generate higher pressure to pump blood around the entire body, whereas the right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs.

Key Fact

The heart has four chambers. Blood flows: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

Valves in the heart prevent the backflow of blood. The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with the oxygenated blood it needs to keep beating.

Blood Vessels

There are three types of blood vessel:

  • Arteries — carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick, muscular, elastic walls.
  • Veins — carry blood back to the heart at low pressure. They have thinner walls and contain valves to prevent backflow.
  • Capillaries — tiny vessels that connect arteries to veins. Their walls are one cell thick, allowing efficient exchange of substances (oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide) with body tissues.

Blood Components

Blood is a tissue made up of four components:

  • Red blood cells — contain haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen. They have a biconcave disc shape to increase surface area and no nucleus to carry more haemoglobin.
  • White blood cells — part of the immune system. Phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies.
  • Platelets — cell fragments that help blood to clot at wound sites, forming a scab to prevent blood loss and infection.
  • Plasma — the liquid part of blood. It transports dissolved substances including carbon dioxide, urea, hormones and glucose.

Coronary heart disease (CHD) occurs when layers of fatty material (atheroma) build up inside the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. This can cause a heart attack if the heart muscle does not receive enough oxygen.

Treatments include: stents (wire mesh tubes inserted to hold the artery open), statins (drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels and slow the build-up of fatty deposits), and in severe cases, heart transplants or artificial hearts (mechanical devices that keep blood flowing while waiting for a transplant).

Key Fact

Coronary heart disease is caused by fatty deposits narrowing the coronary arteries. Treatments include stents (hold arteries open), statins (lower cholesterol), heart transplants and artificial hearts.

Stents are effective but carry risks of infection and blood clots. Statins must be taken long-term and can cause side effects such as headaches and muscle pain. Artificial hearts are temporary and can cause blood clots or infection. Heart transplants are limited by donor availability and the risk of rejection by the immune system.

biology-paper-1.title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues
biology-paper-1.description: Risk factors for non-communicable diseases, cancer, and how plant tissues are organised.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
Health and Disease

Health is a state of physical and mental wellbeing. Disease is a condition where part of the body does not function properly. Diseases can be communicable (caused by pathogens and spread between people) or non-communicable (not caused by pathogens and cannot be passed on). Sometimes diseases interact — for example, immune system conditions can make a person more susceptible to communicable diseases.

Key Fact

Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are not caused by pathogens and cannot be spread. Major NCDs include cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, lung disease and cancer. Risk factors include smoking, obesity, alcohol and lack of exercise.

Risk Factors for Non-Communicable Diseases

A risk factor is something that increases the probability of developing a disease. Key risk factors include:

  • Smoking — linked to lung cancer, cardiovascular disease and lung disease.
  • Obesity — a risk factor for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
  • Alcohol — linked to liver disease and some cancers.
  • Lack of exercise — increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and obesity.

It is important to understand the difference between a risk factor and a cause. Risk factors are correlated with disease — they make disease more likely — but correlation does not always prove causation.

Cancer is caused by changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division. Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells contained in one area — they do not invade other tissues. Malignant tumours invade neighbouring tissues and can spread to other parts of the body through the blood, forming secondary tumours — this is known as metastasis.

Risk factors for cancer include genetic factors, ionising radiation (e.g. UV light), certain viruses (e.g. HPV), and lifestyle factors such as smoking and obesity.

Plant Tissues and Organ Systems

Plants are also organised into tissues and organs. The main plant tissues include:

  • Epidermal tissue — covers the surface of the plant for protection.
  • Palisade mesophyll — packed with chloroplasts and located near the top of the leaf where it receives the most light for photosynthesis.
  • Spongy mesophyll — has air spaces that allow gases (\(CO_2\) and \(O_2\)) to diffuse easily.
  • Xylem — xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves. It is made of hollow, dead cells with lignified walls.
  • Phloem — phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant in a process called translocation.
Key Fact

Xylem transports water and minerals upwards (transpiration stream). Phloem transports dissolved sugars to where they are needed (translocation). Xylem cells are dead and hollow; phloem cells are living.

Transpiration is the evaporation and diffusion of water from the surface of leaves, mainly through the stomata. This creates a continuous transpiration stream that pulls water up through the xylem from the roots. The rate of transpiration is affected by temperature, humidity, air movement and light intensity.

biology-paper-1.title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences
biology-paper-1.description: Covers what are communicable diseases?, types of pathogens, how diseases spread and more.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
What Are Communicable Diseases?

Communicable diseases are illnesses that can be spread from one organism to another. They are caused by pathogens — harmful microorganisms that invade the body and cause infection.

Key Fact

There are four main types of pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protists. Each type causes disease in different ways and requires different treatments.

Types of Pathogens

Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can reproduce rapidly inside the body. Some bacteria cause disease by producing toxins that damage tissues. Examples include food poisoning (Salmonella) and gonorrhoea (a sexually transmitted infection).

Bacterial infections can be treated with antibiotics, which kill bacteria or stop them from reproducing.

Viruses are not cells — they are much smaller than bacteria and can only reproduce inside living cells. They take over the cell’s machinery to make copies of themselves, often destroying the cell in the process. Examples include measles, HIV, and tobacco mosaic virus in plants.

Viral infections cannot be treated with antibiotics. Instead, the body’s immune system must fight them off, though antiviral drugs can help in some cases.

Fungi and protists are the other two types of pathogens. Fungi like athlete’s foot affect the skin, while protists such as the malaria parasite are often spread by vectors like mosquitoes.

How Diseases Spread

Pathogens can be transmitted (spread) between organisms in several ways:

  • Air: Droplets containing pathogens are released when infected people cough, sneeze, or talk. These can be breathed in by others.
  • Water: Contaminated water can contain pathogens that cause diseases like cholera.
  • Direct contact: Some diseases spread through touching infected surfaces or direct skin contact.
  • Vectors: Animals like mosquitoes can carry pathogens from one host to another.
Key Fact

The spread of communicable diseases can be reduced by hygiene measures, destroying vectors, isolation of infected individuals, and vaccination.

The Body’s Defence Systems

The human body has evolved several defence mechanisms to protect against pathogens. These work as barriers to prevent pathogens entering, or as immune responses to destroy them once inside.

Non-Specific Defences

The body’s first line of defence includes physical and chemical barriers:

  • Skin: Acts as a physical barrier to prevent pathogens entering the body
  • Nose: Contains hairs and mucus that trap particles and pathogens
  • Trachea and bronchi: Lined with cells that produce mucus to trap pathogens, and have cilia that sweep mucus upward
  • Stomach: Produces hydrochloric acid that kills many pathogens in food and drink

The Immune System

If pathogens get past the body’s barriers, the immune system provides the second line of defence. This involves white blood cells that can detect and destroy pathogens.

Phagocytosis: Some white blood cells engulf and digest pathogens. This is a non-specific response that works against any pathogen.

Antibody production: Other white blood cells produce antibodies. These are proteins that bind to specific antigens on the surface of pathogens.

Antitoxin production: White blood cells can also produce antitoxins that neutralise the toxins released by some bacteria.

Memory Cells and Immunity

When white blood cells encounter a pathogen for the first time, some become memory cells. These remain in the blood for many years and provide immunity.

If the same pathogen enters the body again, memory cells quickly recognise it and produce antibodies much faster than the first time. This rapid response often prevents symptoms of disease from developing — the person is immune.

Primary response: When first exposed to a pathogen, it takes several days for white blood cells to recognise it and start producing the right antibodies. During this time, the person may become ill.

Secondary response: Memory cells enable a much faster and stronger antibody response on second exposure. This usually prevents illness.

Vaccination

Vaccination involves introducing small amounts of dead or inactive pathogens into the body. This stimulates white blood cells to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing disease.

If the person is later infected with the live pathogen, their memory cells will recognise it and quickly produce antibodies. This provides immunity without having to suffer from the disease first.

Key Fact

Vaccination programmes have successfully reduced the incidence of many diseases. However, vaccines need to be updated regularly for diseases like flu because the pathogens mutate and change their antigens.

Antibiotics and Drug Resistance

Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them reproducing. They have dramatically reduced deaths from bacterial infections since their discovery. However, antibiotics do not work against viruses.

The overuse and misuse of antibiotics has led to the evolution of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. These “superbugs” are difficult to treat and pose a serious threat to human health.

To slow the development of antibiotic resistance:

  • Doctors should only prescribe antibiotics for bacterial infections
  • Patients must complete the full course of antibiotics, even if they feel better
  • New antibiotics need to be developed to replace those that no longer work

biology-paper-1.title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development
biology-paper-1.description: How vaccines and antibiotics work, antibiotic resistance, and the stages of drug testing.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
Vaccination

A vaccination introduces a small quantity of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body. This stimulates the white blood cells (lymphocytes) to produce antibodies. If the same pathogen enters the body again in the future, the white blood cells can respond rapidly and produce the correct antibodies much faster, preventing infection.

Key Fact

Vaccines stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies by introducing dead or weakened pathogens. Memory lymphocytes remain, allowing a rapid secondary immune response if the pathogen is encountered again.

If a large proportion of the population is vaccinated, the spread of the pathogen is greatly reduced because there are fewer people who can become infected and pass it on. This is called herd immunity.

Antibiotics and Painkillers

Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or prevent them from reproducing inside the body. They are used to treat bacterial infections. Antibiotics do not work on viruses because viruses reproduce inside the host’s own cells, and it is very difficult to damage the virus without also damaging the host cell.

Painkillers treat the symptoms of disease (e.g. pain, inflammation) but do not kill pathogens. They make the patient feel better but do not cure the infection itself.

Some bacteria have developed antibiotic resistance through natural selection. Mutations in bacterial DNA can produce strains that are not killed by an antibiotic. These resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance gene. Overuse of antibiotics and failure to complete courses accelerates this process.

MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is an example of a “superbug” that is resistant to several antibiotics. To reduce the development of resistant strains, doctors should only prescribe antibiotics when necessary, patients should always complete the full course, and the agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted.

Drug Development and Testing

New drugs must go through rigorous testing before they can be used. The stages are:

Stage 1 — Preclinical testing: The drug is tested on cells, tissues and live animals. This checks for toxicity (is it safe?), efficacy (does it work?) and dose (how much is needed?).

Stage 2 — Clinical trials: If preclinical tests are successful, the drug is tested on healthy volunteers and then on patients. A very low dose is given first to check for side effects. Double-blind trials are used where neither the patient nor the doctor knows who receives the real drug and who receives a placebo (an inactive substance). This eliminates bias.

Stage 3 — Peer review and approval: Results are reviewed by independent scientists and regulatory bodies before the drug is approved for widespread use.

Key Fact

Drug testing stages: preclinical (cells, tissues, animals) → clinical trials (healthy volunteers, then patients, using double-blind placebo trials) → peer review and approval. This process typically takes over 10 years.

Many drugs were originally discovered in plants or microorganisms. For example, the painkiller aspirin was originally derived from willow bark, the heart drug digitalis comes from foxgloves, and the antibiotic penicillin was discovered from a mould by Alexander Fleming in 1928.

biology-paper-1.title: Photosynthesis and Respiration
biology-paper-1.description: The equations and limiting factors for photosynthesis, plus aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
biology-paper-1.content_html:
Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction that takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells. It uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. The word equation is:

$$\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$$

The balanced symbol equation is:

$$6CO_2 + 6H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{light}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$$

Key Fact

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). It takes place in the chloroplasts and requires light energy absorbed by chlorophyll.

The rate of photosynthesis is affected by three limiting factors:

  • Light intensity — as light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases until another factor becomes limiting.
  • Carbon dioxide concentration — increasing \(CO_2\) increases the rate until another factor limits it.
  • Temperature — higher temperatures increase the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions up to an optimum, beyond which enzymes denature and the rate drops sharply.

These limiting factors interact, and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis at a given time. Light intensity follows an inverse square law — it is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source: \(\text{light intensity} \propto \frac{1}{d^2}\). You may need to explain graphs of photosynthesis rate involving two or three limiting factors simultaneously.

Plants use the glucose produced during photosynthesis for several purposes: respiration (to release energy), converting glucose to starch for storage, producing cellulose for cell walls, producing amino acids (by combining with nitrate ions from the soil) for protein synthesis, and producing lipids (fats and oils) for storage in seeds.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration is an exothermic reaction that takes place continuously in all living cells. It occurs in the mitochondria and requires oxygen. The word equation is:

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$$

The balanced symbol equation is:

$$C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O$$

Key Fact

Aerobic respiration: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\). It is exothermic, occurs in mitochondria, and releases energy for life processes including muscle contraction, maintaining body temperature and building molecules.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is not available. It releases much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration because glucose is only partially broken down.

In animals: \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}\)

In plants and yeast (fermentation): \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}\)

During intense exercise, the muscles cannot get enough oxygen for aerobic respiration, so anaerobic respiration occurs alongside it. This produces lactic acid, which builds up in the muscles and causes fatigue and cramp. After exercise, you continue to breathe heavily to repay the oxygen debt — the extra oxygen needed to break down the accumulated lactic acid.

Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver where it is converted back into glucose. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.

During exercise, the body responds to the increased demand for energy: heart rate increases, breathing rate and depth increase, and blood is redirected to the muscles. These changes supply more oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration and remove more carbon dioxide.

biology-paper-2.title: Homeostasis and the Nervous System
biology-paper-2.description: How the body maintains stable internal conditions, and the structure of the nervous system.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Homeostasis

Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of the body to maintain a stable environment. This is essential because cells need the right conditions to function properly — particularly for enzyme action. The conditions controlled include body temperature, blood glucose concentration, water levels and ion levels.

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains optimal internal conditions for enzyme activity. All control systems involve: receptors (detect stimuli), coordination centres (brain, spinal cord, pancreas) and effectors (muscles or glands that produce a response).

Homeostatic control systems involve three components: receptors that detect changes in the environment (stimuli), coordination centres (the brain, spinal cord and pancreas) that receive and process information, and effectors (muscles and glands) that carry out a response. Many homeostatic systems use negative feedback — a mechanism where the response works to reverse the change and return conditions to the optimum.

The Nervous System

The nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and coordinate behaviour. It is made up of the central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord — and the peripheral nervous system (sensory and motor neurones that connect receptors and effectors to the CNS).

The pathway of a nervous response is: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in CNS) → motor neurone → effector → response.

Neurones do not directly touch each other. The tiny gap between two neurones is called a synapse. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of a neurone, it triggers the release of chemical neurotransmitters that diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse. This allows signals to pass between neurones.

Reflex Actions

Reflex actions are rapid, automatic responses that do not involve the conscious part of the brain. They protect the body from harm — for example, pulling your hand away from a hot object. The nerve pathway for a reflex is called a reflex arc:

Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector

Key Fact

Reflex arcs bypass the brain, making responses faster. The pathway is: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector. This protects the body from danger.

Required Practical 7 involves investigating the effect of a factor on human reaction time. A common method is the ruler drop test: one person holds a ruler vertically, the other person catches it when released. The distance the ruler falls is related to reaction time — a shorter distance means a faster reaction. Variables such as caffeine, practice, or distraction can be investigated as independent variables.

The brain is the main coordination centre. It receives impulses from receptors and sends impulses to effectors. Different regions of the brain have different functions: the cerebral cortex (consciousness, thought, memory), the cerebellum (balance and coordination) and the medulla (unconscious activities like breathing and heart rate).

biology-paper-2.title: The Endocrine System and Blood Glucose Control
biology-paper-2.description: How hormones coordinate body functions, and how the pancreas controls blood glucose levels.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
The Endocrine System

The endocrine system is made up of glands that produce hormones. Hormones are chemical messengers secreted directly into the blood and carried to target organs where they produce an effect. Compared to the nervous system, hormonal responses are slower but longer-lasting and act on a wider area.

The pituitary gland in the brain is called the “master gland” because it produces hormones that act on other glands, stimulating them to release their own hormones. Key endocrine glands include:

  • Pituitary gland (brain) — produces growth hormone, FSH, LH, ADH, TSH.
  • Thyroid gland (neck) — produces thyroxine, which regulates metabolic rate.
  • Pancreas — produces insulin and glucagon to control blood glucose.
  • Adrenal glands (above kidneys) — produce adrenaline for the “fight or flight” response.
  • Ovaries — produce oestrogen and progesterone.
  • Testes — produce testosterone.
Key Fact

The pituitary gland is the “master gland” — it produces hormones that control other glands. Hormones travel in the blood to target organs and produce slower but longer-lasting responses than nerves.

Blood Glucose Control

Blood glucose concentration is monitored and controlled by the pancreas. When blood glucose rises (e.g. after eating), the pancreas releases insulin. Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into cells, and stimulates the liver to convert glucose into glycogen for storage. This lowers blood glucose back to normal.

When blood glucose falls too low (e.g. during exercise or between meals), the pancreas releases glucagon. Glucagon causes the liver to convert glycogen back into glucose, which is released into the blood. This raises blood glucose back to normal. This is a classic example of negative feedback.

Key Fact

Insulin lowers blood glucose (glucose → glycogen in liver). Glucagon raises blood glucose (glycogen → glucose from liver). Both are produced by the pancreas in a negative feedback loop.

Type 1 diabetes is a condition where the pancreas produces little or no insulin. It is usually diagnosed in childhood, is not linked to lifestyle, and is treated with insulin injections. The patient must also monitor their diet and blood glucose levels.

Type 2 diabetes is where the body’s cells no longer respond to insulin properly (insulin resistance). It is linked to obesity and lifestyle factors. It is treated with a carbohydrate-controlled diet, increased exercise and sometimes medication. Type 2 diabetes is becoming more common worldwide due to rising obesity levels.

The nervous system transmits electrical impulses along neurones for fast, short-lived, localised responses. The endocrine system uses hormones carried in the blood for slower, longer-lasting, widespread responses. Both systems work together to coordinate body functions — for example, the hypothalamus in the brain links the two systems.

biology-paper-2.title: Hormones in Reproduction and Contraception
biology-paper-2.description: The menstrual cycle hormones, hormonal and non-hormonal contraception, and fertility treatments.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Hormones and the Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle is a roughly 28-day cycle controlled by four key hormones that interact through feedback mechanisms:

  • FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) — released by the pituitary gland. It causes an egg to mature in a follicle in the ovary and stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen.
  • Oestrogen — produced by the ovaries. It causes the uterus lining to thicken and build up with blood vessels. At high levels, it stimulates LH release and inhibits FSH.
  • LH (luteinising hormone) — released by the pituitary gland. A surge of LH triggers ovulation around day 14.
  • Progesterone — produced by the empty follicle after ovulation. It maintains the uterus lining. If no fertilisation occurs, progesterone levels drop, the lining breaks down, and menstruation begins.
Key Fact

The menstrual cycle: FSH (matures egg + stimulates oestrogen) → Oestrogen (thickens lining + triggers LH surge) → LH (triggers ovulation on day 14) → Progesterone (maintains lining). All four hormones interact via feedback.

Contraception

Contraception can be hormonal or non-hormonal:

Oral contraceptive pill — contains hormones (oestrogen and/or progesterone) that inhibit FSH production, preventing egg maturation and ovulation. The combined pill uses both hormones; the progesterone-only pill has fewer side effects.

Contraceptive injection, implant or skin patch — release progesterone slowly over weeks or months, providing long-term contraception without daily action.

Intrauterine device (IUD) — a device inserted into the uterus. Hormonal IUDs release progesterone; copper IUDs are non-hormonal and prevent implantation.

Barrier methods — condoms (male and female) and diaphragms physically prevent sperm from reaching the egg. Condoms also protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs).

Spermicidal agents — chemicals that kill or disable sperm, often used with barrier methods.

Surgical methods — sterilisation (cutting or tying the fallopian tubes or vas deferens) is permanent and very effective.

Abstinence or natural family planning — avoiding intercourse during the fertile window. Less reliable than other methods.

Key Fact

Hormonal contraceptives work by inhibiting FSH (preventing egg maturation) and/or preventing ovulation. Only barrier methods (condoms) protect against both pregnancy and STIs.

Fertility Treatments

Some couples have difficulty conceiving. Fertility treatments include:

  • FSH and LH injections — given to women who do not produce enough FSH naturally, stimulating egg maturation and ovulation.
  • IVF (in vitro fertilisation) — the mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate multiple eggs, which are collected and fertilised with sperm outside the body. One or two embryos are then transferred to the uterus.

IVF raises ethical issues: it is emotionally and physically demanding, expensive, has a low success rate, and can result in multiple pregnancies. Unused embryos may be destroyed, which some people object to on moral or religious grounds.

biology-paper-2.title: Reproduction, Meiosis and DNA
biology-paper-2.description: Sexual and asexual reproduction, how meiosis produces gametes, and the structure of DNA.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Sexual and Asexual Reproduction

There are two types of reproduction. Sexual reproduction involves the fusion (joining) of male and female gametes (sperm and egg). The offspring are genetically different from each other and from both parents, because they receive a random mix of genetic material. This genetic variation is important for natural selection.

Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes. The offspring are genetically identical to the parent — they are clones. Asexual reproduction occurs through mitosis. Many plants and some animals (e.g. bacteria, starfish) can reproduce asexually.

Key Fact

Sexual reproduction: two parents, gametes fuse, offspring are genetically varied. Asexual reproduction: one parent, mitosis only, offspring are clones. Variation in sexual reproduction is important for natural selection and survival.

Meiosis

Meiosis is the type of cell division that produces gametes (sex cells). It takes place in the reproductive organs (ovaries and testes). Before meiosis, the DNA replicates. The cell then divides twice, producing four genetically different haploid cells, each with half the chromosome number (23 in humans).

When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the full chromosome number is restored (46 in humans). The resulting cell is called a zygote, which then divides by mitosis to form an embryo.

Mitosis: one division, produces 2 identical diploid cells, used for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, produces 4 different haploid cells (gametes), used for sexual reproduction. Both start with DNA replication, but meiosis shuffles genetic material, creating variation.

DNA Structure

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made up of two strands twisted into a double helix. DNA is found in the nucleus of cells, arranged into structures called chromosomes. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total).

A gene is a short section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, which are assembled into a specific protein. The entire set of genetic material in an organism is called its genome.

Key Fact

DNA is a double helix found in chromosomes in the nucleus. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. The Human Genome Project mapped all human DNA.

The Human Genome Project was an international effort to map every gene in the human genome. Understanding the genome helps scientists identify genes linked to specific diseases, develop personalised medicines, and trace human migration patterns and evolutionary relationships.

biology-paper-2.title: Genetic Inheritance and Inherited Disorders
biology-paper-2.description: Dominant and recessive alleles, Punnett squares, and inherited conditions like cystic fibrosis.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Alleles and Inheritance

Most characteristics are controlled by several genes working together (polygenic). Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene with two forms called alleles. You inherit one allele from each parent, giving you two alleles for each gene.

If the two alleles are the same, the individual is homozygous for that gene. If they are different, the individual is heterozygous. A dominant allele is always expressed when present (shown by a capital letter, e.g. B). A recessive allele is only expressed when two copies are present (bb).

Key Fact

Genotype = the combination of alleles (e.g. Bb). Phenotype = the physical characteristic expressed (e.g. brown eyes). Dominant alleles only need one copy to be expressed; recessive alleles need two copies (homozygous recessive).

Punnett Squares and Genetic Diagrams

A Punnett square is used to show the possible combinations of alleles in offspring. For example, if both parents are heterozygous (Bb):

The offspring ratios would be: \(\frac{1}{4}\) BB, \(\frac{2}{4}\) Bb, \(\frac{1}{4}\) bb. This gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio (3 dominant : 1 recessive).

A couple are both carriers of cystic fibrosis (genotype Ff). What is the probability of their child having cystic fibrosis?

Parent genotypes: Ff × Ff. The Punnett square gives: FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Only ff has cystic fibrosis. So the probability is \(\frac{1}{4}\) or 25%. Note: each child has the same probability, regardless of previous children.

Inherited Disorders

Some disorders are caused by faulty alleles inherited from parents:

Cystic fibrosis is a disorder of cell membranes caused by a recessive allele (f). A person must inherit two copies (ff) to be affected. A carrier (Ff) has one copy but does not show symptoms. It causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system.

Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele. It causes extra fingers or toes. Only one copy of the dominant allele is needed to have the condition (Dd or DD).

Key Fact

Cystic fibrosis = recessive disorder (need ff to be affected; Ff = carrier). Polydactyly = dominant disorder (need only one D allele). Use Punnett squares to predict offspring ratios.

During IVF, embryos can be screened for genetic disorders before being implanted. This allows parents to select embryos that do not carry the faulty allele. However, embryo screening is controversial — some people argue it prevents suffering, while others believe it is unethical to select embryos or that it could lead to “designer babies.”

Sex Determination

In humans, sex is determined by the 23rd pair of chromosomes: XX = female, XY = male. A Punnett square shows there is a 50% chance of each sex. The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene, which triggers male development.

biology-paper-2.title: Variation, Evolution and Natural Selection
biology-paper-2.description: The causes of variation, Darwin’s theory of natural selection, and evidence for evolution.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Variation

Variation is the differences between individuals of the same species. It can be caused by:

  • Genetic variation — differences in DNA inherited from parents. Caused by sexual reproduction (meiosis shuffles genes) and mutations (random changes in DNA).
  • Environmental variation — differences caused by the conditions an organism lives in, e.g. diet, climate, lifestyle.
  • Combination — most characteristics (e.g. height, weight) are influenced by both genes and environment.
Key Fact

Variation is caused by genetics (inherited from parents), the environment (conditions), or both. Mutations are random changes in DNA that can introduce new alleles. Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype.

Evolution by Natural Selection

Evolution is the gradual change in inherited characteristics of a population over many generations. Charles Darwin proposed the theory of natural selection to explain how evolution occurs:

  1. Within a population, there is variation in characteristics due to genetic differences.
  2. Individuals with characteristics better suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest).
  3. These individuals pass on the advantageous alleles to their offspring.
  4. Over many generations, the proportion of individuals with the advantageous characteristic increases.

Evidence for evolution comes from: fossils (show how organisms have changed over time), antibiotic-resistant bacteria (observed natural selection in action), and comparative anatomy (similar bone structures in different species suggest common ancestors). The fossil record is incomplete because not all organisms fossilise, and many fossils are destroyed by geological processes.

Key Fact

Natural selection: variation → survival of the fittest → advantageous alleles passed on → frequency increases over generations. Evidence includes fossils, resistant bacteria and comparative anatomy.

Selective Breeding and Extinction

Selective breeding (artificial selection) is when humans choose organisms with desirable traits to breed together. Examples include breeding cows for higher milk yield, dogs for specific characteristics, and crops for disease resistance. A disadvantage is that it reduces genetic variation within the population, making it more vulnerable to disease.

Extinction occurs when a species dies out completely. Causes include: new predators or diseases, environmental changes, loss of habitat, competition, and catastrophic events. Carl Linnaeus developed the classification system that organises living things into groups based on shared characteristics: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

biology-paper-2.title: Genetic Engineering and Ecology
biology-paper-2.description: Covers genetic engineering (4.6.4), benefits and risks of genetic engineering, ecosystems and com...
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Genetic Engineering

Genetic engineering is a process where scientists modify the genetic material of an organism. A gene that codes for a useful characteristic is “cut” from one organism’s DNA and inserted into another organism’s genome. The organism that receives the new gene is called a genetically modified organism (GMO).

Key Fact

In genetic engineering, enzymes are used to isolate the required gene. This gene is then inserted into a vector (such as a bacterial plasmid or virus) which carries it into the cells of the target organism. The organism’s cells then produce the desired protein.

The process of genetic engineering follows a clear sequence of steps. First, the gene that produces the desired characteristic is identified and isolated using restriction enzymes, which cut DNA at specific recognition sequences. The gene is then inserted into a vector — typically a small ring of bacterial DNA called a plasmid. The vector carries the gene into the host organism’s cells, where it is incorporated into the DNA and expressed to produce the desired protein.

One of the most important applications is the production of human insulin by genetically modified bacteria. The human insulin gene is inserted into bacterial plasmids, and the bacteria then produce insulin in large quantities. This replaced the older method of extracting insulin from pig or cow pancreases, which sometimes caused allergic reactions in patients.

GM crops have been engineered to be resistant to insect attack or to produce higher yields. For example, Bt corn contains a gene from a soil bacterium that produces a natural insecticide, reducing the need for chemical pesticides. Golden rice has been modified to produce beta-carotene (a source of vitamin A) to help combat vitamin A deficiency in developing countries.

Benefits and Risks of Genetic Engineering

Genetic engineering has significant potential benefits. In agriculture, GM crops can increase food production by improving resistance to pests, disease and herbicides. This can help feed a growing world population. In medicine, genetic engineering allows large-scale production of useful proteins such as insulin and growth hormone.

However, there are concerns. Some people worry that GM crops could have unknown effects on human health if consumed over long periods. There are also ecological concerns — genes from GM plants could spread to wild populations through cross-pollination, potentially creating “superweeds” that are resistant to herbicides. Ethical concerns exist about whether it is right to modify the genes of living organisms, particularly when it comes to genetic modification of animals or potential future modifications of human embryos.

Key Fact

You are expected to evaluate the benefits and risks of genetic engineering. Benefits include: disease-resistant crops, higher yields, medical protein production. Risks include: unknown long-term health effects, gene transfer to wild populations, and ethical concerns.

Ecosystems and Communities

An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. Ecosystems can range in size from a small pond to an entire ocean. Within an ecosystem, organisms are organised into levels.

A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting together in an area. A population is all the organisms of one species in a given area. A habitat is the place where an organism lives. Each species has its own role within the community, known as its niche.

Abiotic factors are non-living conditions that influence where organisms can live. These include light intensity, temperature, moisture level, soil pH and mineral content, wind speed and direction, and carbon dioxide levels (for plants) or oxygen levels (for aquatic organisms).

Biotic factors are living factors that affect organisms in an ecosystem. These include availability of food, the introduction of new predators or competitors, and the arrival of new pathogens (disease-causing organisms). Changes in any biotic or abiotic factor can affect the distribution and population size of species in a community.

Competition and Interdependence

Organisms within a community compete for resources. Animals compete for food, territory, mates and water. Plants compete for light, water, space and mineral ions from the soil. If two species are competing for the same niche, one will usually out-compete the other. Within a community, species depend on each other for food, shelter, seed dispersal and pollination — this is called interdependence. If one species is removed, the whole community can be affected.

A stable community is one where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain roughly the same. Examples include tropical rainforests and ancient oak woodlands. In these ecosystems, the populations of predators and prey, producers and consumers are balanced over time.

Feeding Relationships and Trophic Levels

Trophic levels describe the position of an organism in a food chain. Producers (usually green plants or algae) are at trophic level 1 — they photosynthesise to make their own food. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat the producers and are at trophic level 2. Secondary consumers (carnivores) eat the primary consumers and are at trophic level 3. Tertiary consumers are at trophic level 4.

Key Fact

Producers are the starting point of all food chains because they transfer energy from the Sun into biomass through photosynthesis. All consumers depend — directly or indirectly — on producers for their energy.

Predators kill and eat other animals (their prey). In a stable community, the populations of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles. When the prey population increases, more food is available for predators, so the predator population also increases. This then causes the prey population to fall (more are eaten), which in turn causes the predator population to decline. This repeating pattern is known as the predator-prey cycle.

Decomposers (mainly bacteria and fungi) break down dead plant and animal matter through the process of decay. This returns mineral ions and nutrients to the soil, where they can be taken up again by plants. Decomposition is faster in warm, moist, aerobic conditions. Decomposers are essential for nutrient cycling in ecosystems.

Energy is transferred along food chains, but not all energy passes from one trophic level to the next. At each level, energy is lost to the surroundings through life processes — organisms use energy for movement, keeping warm, and other metabolic reactions. Energy is also lost in waste products (faeces and urine) and through respiration. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels — there is not enough energy left to support organisms beyond that point.

biology-paper-2.title: Ecosystems, Biodiversity and Human Impact
biology-paper-2.description: Food chains, nutrient cycling, biodiversity, and how human activities affect ecosystems.
biology-paper-2.content_html:
Communities and Ecosystems

An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic factors) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. A community includes all the organisms of different species living together. A population is all the organisms of one species in a habitat.

Abiotic factors include light intensity, temperature, moisture, soil pH and mineral content, wind speed and direction, and availability of carbon dioxide and oxygen. Biotic factors include availability of food, new predators, new pathogens and competition between organisms.

Key Fact

Ecosystems consist of biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) factors. In a stable community, the populations of all species are balanced. Changes to abiotic or biotic factors can destabilise a community.

Food Chains and Interdependence

Organisms in a community depend on each other for food, shelter and other resources. This is called interdependence. Food chains show the flow of energy from producers to consumers:

Producer → Primary consumer → Secondary consumer → Tertiary consumer

Producers (plants) convert light energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis. Consumers obtain energy by eating other organisms. If one species in a food chain is removed, it affects all the other organisms — this is called interdependence.

Carbon is recycled through ecosystems. Plants take in \(CO_2\) for photosynthesis and use it to make glucose. Animals eat plants and release \(CO_2\) through respiration. When organisms die, decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the dead material, releasing \(CO_2\) through respiration. Combustion of fossil fuels also releases \(CO_2\).

Biodiversity and Human Impact

Biodiversity is the variety of different species in an ecosystem. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable and resilient to change. However, human activities are rapidly reducing biodiversity worldwide.

Human activities that reduce biodiversity include:

  • Deforestation — clearing forests for agriculture and building destroys habitats.
  • Pollution — land, water and air pollution damage habitats and kill organisms.
  • Global warming — rising temperatures alter habitats and cause species migration or extinction.
  • Overexploitation — overfishing, hunting and intensive farming reduce populations.
Key Fact

Biodiversity is being reduced by deforestation, pollution, global warming and overexploitation. Conservation programmes, breeding programmes, seed banks and habitat restoration help maintain biodiversity.

Strategies to maintain biodiversity include: breeding programmes for endangered species, protection of rare habitats (e.g. national parks, SSSIs), reintroduction of hedgerows and field margins in agricultural areas, seed banks to preserve genetic diversity, and reducing deforestation and carbon emissions. Scientists also use techniques like quadrats and transects to sample and monitor biodiversity in ecosystems.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom
chemistry-paper-1.description: Covers what are atoms?, elements and the periodic table, compounds and chemical formulas and more.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
What are Atoms?

Everything around us is made up of tiny particles called atoms. Atoms are incredibly small — about 0.1 nanometres across. To put this in perspective, if an atom was the size of a football, a football would be the size of Earth!

Key Fact

All substances are made of atoms. Atoms cannot be created or destroyed in chemical reactions.

Atoms are made up of three types of particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons. Understanding how these particles are arranged helps us understand how different elements behave and react with each other.

Elements and the Periodic Table

An element is a pure substance that contains only one type of atom. For example, oxygen contains only oxygen atoms, and carbon contains only carbon atoms. There are about 100 different elements, and they’re all organised in the periodic table.

Each element has a unique atomic number. This tells us how many protons are in each atom of that element. Hydrogen has atomic number 1 (1 proton), helium has atomic number 2 (2 protons), and so on.

Elements in the same column (group) of the periodic table have similar properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell. This affects how they react with other elements.

Compounds and Chemical Formulas

When atoms of different elements join together, they form compounds. For example, water (\(H_2O\)) is a compound made from hydrogen and oxygen atoms. The chemical formula tells us exactly which atoms are present and in what ratio.

Key Fact

In chemical formulas, the small numbers (subscripts) tell us how many atoms of each element are present. \(H_2O\) means 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

Common compounds you should know include:

  • Water: \(H_2O\) (hydrogen and oxygen)
  • Carbon dioxide: \(CO_2\) (carbon and oxygen)
  • Sodium chloride: \(NaCl\) (sodium and chlorine)
  • Methane: \(CH_4\) (carbon and hydrogen)

The Structure of the Atom

Modern atomic theory tells us that atoms have a specific structure. At the centre is the nucleus, which contains protons and neutrons. Around the nucleus, electrons move in regions called electron shells or energy levels.

Protons: Positively charged particles in the nucleus. The number of protons determines what element the atom is.

Neutrons: Neutral particles (no charge) in the nucleus. They add mass to the atom but don’t affect its chemical properties.

Electrons: Negatively charged particles that move around the nucleus in shells. They’re involved in chemical bonding.

The relative masses are important to remember: protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1, while electrons have a relative mass of almost zero (1/1836 to be precise).

How the Atomic Model Developed

Our understanding of atomic structure has changed dramatically over time as scientists gathered new evidence. This shows how scientific knowledge develops through experimentation and discovery.

1803

Dalton’s Atomic Theory

John Dalton proposed that all matter was made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms. He thought atoms were like tiny solid spheres.

1897

Discovery of the Electron

J.J. Thomson discovered electrons and proposed the ‘plum pudding’ model — atoms were positive spheres with negative electrons embedded in them.

1909

Rutherford’s Gold Foil Experiment

Ernest Rutherford fired alpha particles at gold foil. Most passed through, but some bounced back, proving atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus.

1913

Bohr’s Model

Niels Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in specific energy levels or shells, like planets around the sun.

Each new discovery built on previous work and led to a better understanding of atomic structure. This is a great example of how scientific knowledge is provisional — it can change when new evidence is discovered.

Mass Number and Atomic Number

Every element can be described using two important numbers. The atomic number tells us how many protons are in the nucleus. The mass number tells us the total number of protons and neutrons.

We can use these numbers to work out the number of each type of particle in an atom:

  • Number of protons = atomic number
  • Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number
  • Number of electrons = number of protons (in a neutral atom)
Key Fact

In a neutral atom, the number of protons always equals the number of electrons. This means the positive and negative charges balance out.

Key Takeaways

  • All matter is made of atoms, which contain protons, neutrons, and electrons arranged with a nucleus at the centre
  • Elements contain only one type of atom, while compounds contain atoms of different elements chemically bonded together
  • Our model of atomic structure has evolved over time as scientists made new discoveries and gathered evidence

chemistry-paper-1.title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups
chemistry-paper-1.description: How elements are arranged in the periodic table and the properties of Groups 1, 7 and 0.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
The Development of the Periodic Table

Before the discovery of protons and neutrons, scientists attempted to classify elements by arranging them in order of atomic weight. Dmitri Mendeleev (1869) arranged elements in order of atomic weight but left gaps for undiscovered elements and swapped some elements so that those with similar properties lined up in the same columns. When elements such as gallium and germanium were later discovered and matched his predictions, his table was widely accepted.

The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of atomic number (not atomic weight). Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, giving them similar chemical properties. Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of electron shells.

Key Fact

Elements are arranged by atomic number. Groups (columns) share the same number of outer electrons and similar properties. Periods (rows) share the same number of electron shells. Metals are on the left; non-metals are on the right.

Group 1 — Alkali Metals

The alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) all have one electron in their outer shell. They are soft, have low density and react vigorously with water, producing a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas:

$$2Na + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + H_2$$

Going down Group 1, reactivity increases because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and is more easily lost (less electrostatic attraction). The elements also have lower melting points and higher densities going down the group.

Group 7 — Halogens

The halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At) have seven electrons in their outer shell. They exist as diatomic molecules (\(Cl_2\), \(Br_2\), etc.) and react with metals to form ionic compounds called halides (e.g. NaCl).

Going down Group 7, reactivity decreases because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder to gain an extra electron. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from its compound, e.g. chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide.

Key Fact

Group 1: reactivity increases down the group (easier to lose outer electron). Group 7: reactivity decreases down the group (harder to gain an electron). These trends are opposite because metals lose electrons while non-metals gain them.

The noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) have full outer electron shells, making them very stable and unreactive. They are used where inert gases are needed: helium in balloons and airships, neon in advertising signs, argon in light bulbs and welding. Boiling point increases down the group.

Transition metals are found in the central block of the periodic table. They have typical metallic properties: high melting points, high density, good conductors. Unlike Group 1 metals, transition metals are less reactive, harder and denser. They form coloured compounds and can act as catalysts (e.g. iron in the Haber process).

chemistry-paper-1.title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding
chemistry-paper-1.description: How atoms bond by transferring or sharing electrons, and the properties of metallic bonds.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Ionic Bonding

When metals react with non-metals, electrons are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom. The metal atom loses electrons to form a positive ion (cation), and the non-metal atom gains electrons to form a negative ion (anion). Both ions then have full outer electron shells and are stable.

The strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. For example, in sodium chloride (NaCl), sodium loses one electron to become \(Na^+\) and chlorine gains one electron to become \(Cl^-\).

Key Fact

Ionic bonding: metal atoms lose electrons (form positive ions) and non-metal atoms gain electrons (form negative ions). The ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction in a giant ionic lattice.

Covalent Bonding

When non-metals bond with other non-metals, they share pairs of electrons. This is called a covalent bond. Each shared pair of electrons counts as one bond. Examples include:

  • \(H_2\) — a single covalent bond (one shared pair).
  • \(O_2\) — a double covalent bond (two shared pairs: \(O=O\)).
  • \(N_2\) — a triple covalent bond (three shared pairs: \(N \equiv N\)).
  • \(H_2O\) — two single covalent bonds.
  • \(CH_4\) — four single covalent bonds.

You need to draw dot-and-cross diagrams showing how electrons are shared or transferred. For ionic bonding, show the transfer of electrons and the charges on the resulting ions. For covalent bonding, show the shared pairs of electrons in the overlap between atoms. Only show outer shell electrons. Use dots for one atom and crosses for the other.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, the outer electrons are delocalised — they leave their atoms and form a “sea” of electrons that can move freely through the structure. The metallic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and this sea of delocalised electrons.

Key Fact

Metallic bonding: positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. This explains why metals conduct electricity (delocalised electrons carry charge) and are malleable (layers of ions can slide over each other).

Ionic: transfer of electrons, metal + non-metal, forms a giant ionic lattice. Covalent: sharing of electrons, non-metal + non-metal, forms simple molecules or giant covalent structures. Metallic: delocalised electrons, metal atoms, forms a giant metallic structure.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Structure, Properties and Carbon Allotropes
chemistry-paper-1.description: Giant ionic lattices, simple molecules, giant covalent structures, and allotropes of carbon.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Properties of Ionic Compounds

Ionic compounds form giant ionic lattices — a regular arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions. The strong electrostatic forces between the ions act in all directions, giving ionic compounds these properties:

  • High melting and boiling points — a lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong ionic bonds.
  • Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved — the ions are free to move and carry charge. They do not conduct when solid because the ions are fixed in position.
Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (strong bonds in all directions), conduct when molten or dissolved (ions free to move), do not conduct when solid (ions fixed in lattice).

Properties of Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecules (e.g. \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\), \(O_2\)) have strong covalent bonds within the molecule but weak intermolecular forces between molecules. This gives them:

  • Low melting and boiling points — little energy is needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces (not the covalent bonds).
  • Do not conduct electricity — no free electrons or ions to carry charge.

As molecules get larger, the intermolecular forces become stronger, so larger molecules tend to have higher boiling points.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures have millions of atoms connected by covalent bonds in a continuous network. They have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken. Examples include diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide.

Diamond: each carbon atom bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral structure. Very hard, high melting point, does not conduct electricity (no free electrons or ions).

Graphite: each carbon bonds to three others, forming flat layers with weak forces between them. The fourth electron is delocalised, allowing graphite to conduct electricity. Layers can slide over each other, making it soft and slippery (useful as a lubricant).

Graphene: a single layer of graphite — one atom thick. It is very strong, light, and an excellent conductor of electricity and heat. Fullerenes (e.g. \(C_{60}\) buckminsterfullerene) are carbon molecules shaped like hollow spheres or tubes. Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with remarkable strength and conductivity.

Key Fact

Diamond: 4 bonds per carbon, very hard, doesn’t conduct. Graphite: 3 bonds per carbon + delocalised electrons, conducts electricity, layers slide. Graphene: single layer of graphite, strongest known material, conducts.

Polymers are very large molecules made up of many repeating units called monomers. They have relatively strong intermolecular forces between the long chains, so they tend to be solid at room temperature. Examples include poly(ethene) and poly(propene).

chemistry-paper-1.title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations
chemistry-paper-1.description: Covers what are moles?, calculating moles from mass, concentration of solutions and more.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
What Are Moles?

A mole is the unit chemists use to count atoms, molecules and ions. Just like a dozen equals 12 items, one mole equals 6.02 × 10²³ particles. This huge number is called Avogadro's constant.

Key Fact
