One mole of any element has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic mass. For example, one mole of carbon (relative atomic mass 12) has a mass of 12g.

The molar mass connects the microscopic world of atoms to the macroscopic world we can measure. For compounds, we add up the relative atomic masses of all atoms present.

Calculating Moles from Mass

The fundamental equation linking moles, mass and molar mass is:

$\text{number of moles} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}$

This can be rearranged to find mass or molar mass depending on what information you're given.

Calculate the number of moles in 44g of carbon dioxide (CO₂).

Step 1: Find the molar mass of CO₂

Carbon: 1 × 12 = 12g/mol

Oxygen: 2 × 16 = 32g/mol

Total molar mass = 12 + 32 = 44g/mol

Step 2: Apply the formula

$\text{moles} = \frac{44}{44} = 1 \text{ mole}$

Concentration of Solutions

When substances dissolve in water, we create solutions. The concentration tells us how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution.

Key Fact

Concentration can be measured in g/dm³ (mass concentration) or mol/dm³ (molar concentration). Both are essential for different types of calculations.

The two main concentration equations you need to know are:

$$\text{concentration (g/dm³)} = \frac{\text{mass of solute (g)}}{\text{volume of solution (dm³)}}$$

$\text{concentration (mol/dm³)} = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution (dm³)}}$

Remember these volume conversions:

  • 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1000 ml = 1 litre
  • To convert cm³ to dm³: divide by 1000
  • To convert dm³ to cm³: multiply by 1000

Calculating Masses in Reactions

Chemical equations show the molar ratios between reactants and products. We can use these ratios along with molar masses to calculate the masses of substances involved in reactions.

The process follows these steps:

  1. Write the balanced chemical equation
  2. Identify the molar ratio from the equation
  3. Calculate moles of the known substance
  4. Use the molar ratio to find moles of unknown substance
  5. Convert moles back to mass using molar mass

Calculate the mass of water produced when 16g of methane burns completely.

$CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O$

Step 1: Calculate moles of methane

Molar mass of CH₄ = 12 + (4 × 1) = 16 g/mol

$\text{moles of CH}_4 = \frac{16}{16} = 1 \text{ mole}$

Step 2: Use molar ratio

From equation: 1 mole CH₄ produces 2 moles H₂O

Therefore: moles of H₂O = 1 × 2 = 2 moles

Step 3: Convert to mass

Molar mass of H₂O = (2 × 1) + 16 = 18 g/mol

$\text{mass of H}_2\text{O} = 2 × 18 = 36\text{g}$

Limiting Reactants

In many reactions, one reactant runs out before the others. This limiting reactant determines how much product can be formed.

To identify the limiting reactant, calculate how many moles of each reactant you have, then compare this to the molar ratios in the balanced equation. The reactant that would be used up first is the limiting reactant.

Common Calculation Mistakes

Students often make errors when working with quantitative chemistry. Always check your balanced equations are correct before starting calculations. Make sure you convert units properly — especially converting cm³ to dm³ for concentration calculations. Remember that molar mass uses the relative atomic mass from the periodic table, and for compounds you must add up all the atoms present.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction
chemistry-paper-1.description: The reactivity series, displacement reactions, and how metals are extracted from their ores.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
The Reactivity Series

Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity — this is called the reactivity series. The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium) react vigorously with water and acids. Less reactive metals (zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold) react more slowly or not at all.

A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from its compound. For example, if iron is placed in copper sulfate solution, the iron displaces the copper:

$$Fe + CuSO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu$$

Key Fact

The reactivity series (most to least reactive): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, C, Zn, Fe, H, Cu, Ag, Au. Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound.

Extraction of Metals

Metals are found in the Earth’s crust, often combined with other elements in ores. The method of extraction depends on the metal’s position in the reactivity series:

  • Metals less reactive than carbon (e.g. iron, copper, zinc) are extracted by reduction with carbon. Carbon is cheaper and more reactive, so it removes the oxygen from the metal oxide.
  • Metals more reactive than carbon (e.g. aluminium, sodium, potassium) must be extracted by electrolysis, which is more expensive because it requires large amounts of electricity.

For example, iron is extracted from iron oxide using carbon in a blast furnace:

$$2Fe_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Fe + 3CO_2$$

Oxidation is the gain of oxygen (or loss of electrons). Reduction is the loss of oxygen (or gain of electrons). Remember: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain. In a displacement reaction, the more reactive metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and the less reactive metal ion is reduced (gains electrons).

Key Fact

Metals below carbon in the reactivity series are extracted by reduction with carbon. Metals above carbon need electrolysis. Oxidation = gain of oxygen / loss of electrons. Reduction = loss of oxygen / gain of electrons.

Recycling metals saves energy (less needed than extraction from ore), reduces the use of limited ore resources, reduces waste going to landfill, and reduces environmental damage from mining and carbon emissions. However, collection and sorting can be difficult, and recycled metals may be impure.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation
chemistry-paper-1.description: Acid-base reactions, the pH scale, neutralisation, and making salts from acids.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Acids, Bases and the pH Scale

An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)) when dissolved in water. A base is a substance that can neutralise an acid. An alkali is a soluble base that produces hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)) in water.

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Acids have a pH below 7, neutral solutions have a pH of 7, and alkalis have a pH above 7. pH can be measured with universal indicator or a pH probe.

Key Fact

Acids produce \(H^+\) ions in water; alkalis produce \(OH^-\) ions. The pH scale: 0–6 = acidic, 7 = neutral, 8–14 = alkaline. Neutralisation: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\).

Neutralisation Reactions

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base. The ionic equation is:

$$H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O$$

The key reactions of acids are:

  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. E.g. \(Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2\)
  • Acid + metal oxide → salt + water. E.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water. E.g. \(NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. E.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\)

The salt produced depends on which acid is used: hydrochloric acid (\(HCl\)) makes chlorides, sulfuric acid (\(H_2SO_4\)) makes sulfates, and nitric acid (\(HNO_3\)) makes nitrates.

To make a pure, dry salt: add an excess of insoluble base or metal oxide to the acid, filter off the excess solid, then evaporate the water from the filtrate to leave salt crystals. This is Required Practical 1.

Key Fact

HCl → chlorides. \(H_2SO_4\) → sulfates. \(HNO_3\) → nitrates. To predict the salt name: metal name + acid type (e.g. magnesium + sulfuric acid = magnesium sulfate).

Strong acids (e.g. hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric acid) fully ionise in water — every acid molecule releases its \(H^+\) ions. Weak acids (e.g. ethanoic acid, citric acid) only partially ionise — an equilibrium is established between ionised and un-ionised molecules. At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Electrolysis
chemistry-paper-1.description: How electrolysis breaks down ionic compounds using electricity, including aluminium extraction.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is the process of using electricity to break down an ionic compound into its elements. The compound being broken down is called the electrolyte and must be either molten or dissolved in water so that the ions are free to move.

The electrolyte is placed between two electrodes: the cathode (negative electrode) attracts positive metal ions, and the anode (positive electrode) attracts negative non-metal ions.

Key Fact

Electrolysis: positive ions (cations) move to the cathode (negative electrode), negative ions (anions) move to the anode (positive electrode). At the cathode, metals are deposited. At the anode, non-metals are released.

At the cathode, positive metal ions gain electrons (reduction) to form metal atoms. At the anode, negative ions lose electrons (oxidation) to form atoms or molecules. Remember: PANIC — Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

Electrolysis of Molten Compounds

When a molten binary ionic compound (e.g. lead bromide, \(PbBr_2\)) is electrolysed:

  • Cathode: \(Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb\) (lead metal is deposited — reduction).
  • Anode: \(2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2 + 2e^-\) (bromine gas is released — oxidation).

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, there are additional \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions from the water. The rules for predicting products at each electrode are:

Cathode: If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen gas is produced. If less reactive than hydrogen, the metal is deposited.

Anode: If a halide ion is present, the halogen is produced. If no halide is present, oxygen is produced (from \(OH^-\) ions).

Extraction of Aluminium

Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, so it is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (\(Al_2O_3\)). The aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point and reduce energy costs.

At the cathode: \(Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al\) (aluminium is deposited).

At the anode: \(2O^{2-} \rightarrow O_2 + 4e^-\) (oxygen is released). The carbon anodes gradually burn away because the oxygen reacts with them at high temperature, so they need regular replacement.

Key Fact

Aluminium extraction: electrolysis of \(Al_2O_3\) dissolved in cryolite. Al deposited at cathode, \(O_2\) at anode. Carbon anodes burn away and need replacing. The process uses large amounts of electricity, making it expensive.

Required Practical 4 involves electrolysing aqueous solutions using inert (carbon or platinum) electrodes. You observe the products at each electrode and test them: hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop, chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, and oxygen relights a glowing splint.

chemistry-paper-1.title: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions
chemistry-paper-1.description: Covers introduction to energy changes, exothermic reactions, endothermic reactions and more.
chemistry-paper-1.content_html:
Introduction to Energy Changes

All chemical reactions involve energy changes. When chemical bonds are broken and new bonds are formed, energy is either released to the surroundings or absorbed from the surroundings. Understanding these energy changes is crucial for predicting how reactions behave and their practical applications.

Key Fact

Energy is required to break chemical bonds and energy is released when new bonds are formed.

Exothermic Reactions

An exothermic reaction is one where energy is released to the surroundings. In these reactions, more energy is released when new bonds form than is needed to break the original bonds. This results in a net release of energy, usually observed as an increase in temperature of the surroundings.

Common exothermic reactions include combustion reactions, such as burning methane: \(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\). Other examples include neutralisation reactions between acids and bases, and many oxidation reactions.

Hand warmers used in winter often contain iron powder that undergoes an exothermic oxidation reaction with oxygen from the air, releasing heat energy.

Endothermic Reactions

An endothermic reaction is one where energy is absorbed from the surroundings. In these reactions, more energy is needed to break the original bonds than is released when new bonds form. This results in a net absorption of energy, usually observed as a decrease in temperature of the surroundings.

Key Fact

In endothermic reactions, the temperature of the surroundings decreases because energy is absorbed from them.

Thermal decomposition reactions are typically endothermic. For example, heating copper carbonate: \(CuCO_3 \rightarrow CuO + CO_2\). The reaction requires continuous heating to proceed.

Sports injury packs often contain ammonium nitrate that dissolves endothermically in water, absorbing heat and cooling the injured area.

Energy Profiles and Activation Energy

Energy profile diagrams show how the energy of reactants and products changes during a chemical reaction. These diagrams help us understand the energy requirements and energy changes involved in chemical processes.

The activation energy is the minimum energy required for reactants to overcome the energy barrier and start reacting. Even exothermic reactions require this initial energy input to break the first bonds and get the reaction started.

Key Fact

All reactions, whether exothermic or endothermic, require activation energy to begin.

Bond Breaking and Bond Making

During chemical reactions, existing bonds in reactant molecules must be broken before new bonds can form in the product molecules. Bond breaking is always an endothermic process — it requires energy input. Bond making is always an exothermic process — it releases energy.

The overall energy change of a reaction depends on the balance between energy required for bond breaking and energy released during bond making. If more energy is released than absorbed, the reaction is exothermic. If more energy is absorbed than released, the reaction is endothermic.

The energy change of a reaction can be calculated using bond energies:

$\text{Energy change} = \text{Energy required to break bonds} - \text{Energy released making bonds}$

If the result is positive, the reaction is endothermic. If negative, the reaction is exothermic.

Practical Applications

Understanding energy changes in chemical reactions has many practical applications. Exothermic reactions are used in heating systems, self-heating food containers, and rocket fuels. Endothermic reactions are used in instant cold packs for sports injuries and in some industrial processes where cooling is required.

In everyday life, we rely on the exothermic combustion of fuels for heating our homes and powering vehicles. The energy released during these reactions provides the thermal energy we need for warmth and the kinetic energy for movement.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory
chemistry-paper-2.description: What affects the speed of chemical reactions, and how collision theory explains reaction rates.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
Rate of Reaction

The rate of reaction measures how quickly reactants are turned into products. It can be calculated by:

$$\text{rate of reaction} = \frac{\text{quantity of reactant used or product formed}}{\text{time taken}}$$

The rate of a chemical reaction can be changed by altering the: temperature, concentration of solutions (or pressure of gases), surface area of solid reactants, or by using a catalyst.

Key Fact

Rate of reaction can be increased by: raising temperature, increasing concentration/pressure, increasing surface area, or using a catalyst. The rate can be measured by collecting gas, measuring mass loss, or timing colour changes.

Collision Theory

Collision theory states that for a reaction to occur, particles must: (1) collide with each other, and (2) collide with sufficient energy. The minimum energy needed for a successful collision is called the activation energy.

Each factor affects the rate by changing the frequency or energy of collisions:

  • Temperature — higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy. They move faster, collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of collisions have energy \(\geq\) activation energy.
  • Concentration / Pressure — more particles in the same volume means more frequent collisions.
  • Surface area — smaller pieces expose more surface, giving more area for collisions to occur.
  • Catalyst — provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful. The catalyst is not used up.
Key Fact

Collision theory: reactions only happen when particles collide with energy ≥ activation energy. Catalysts lower the activation energy — they are not used up and do not appear in the overall equation.

Common methods for measuring rate include: collecting gas in a gas syringe or over water, measuring the loss of mass on a balance (when gas escapes), or timing how long it takes for a solution to become opaque (e.g. sodium thiosulfate “disappearing cross” experiment). On a graph, a steeper curve means a faster rate.

On a graph of volume of gas vs time: the gradient (steepness) at any point represents the rate. A steeper line = faster rate. The line levels off when the reaction is complete (one reactant has been used up). Changing temperature or concentration affects the steepness but not the final volume (if the same amount of reactant is used). Increasing the amount of reactant increases the total gas produced.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium
chemistry-paper-2.description: How some reactions can go in both directions, and what happens at dynamic equilibrium.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
Reversible Reactions

Some chemical reactions are reversible — the products can react to re-form the original reactants. A reversible reaction is shown with a double arrow (\(\rightleftharpoons\)):

$$A + B \rightleftharpoons C + D$$

A simple example is the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride:

$$NH_4Cl \rightleftharpoons NH_3 + HCl$$

When heated, ammonium chloride decomposes into ammonia and hydrogen chloride. When cooled, these gases recombine to form ammonium chloride again.

Key Fact

In a reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic, the reverse reaction is endothermic by the same amount of energy, and vice versa.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction occurs in a closed system (where nothing can enter or leave), it eventually reaches dynamic equilibrium. At equilibrium:

  • The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
  • The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (but are not necessarily equal).
  • The reaction has not stopped — both forward and reverse reactions are still occurring.

If conditions are changed, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change (Le Chatelier’s principle):

  • Temperature: Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Decreasing temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • Concentration: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products. Increasing the concentration of a product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Pressure (gases only): Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas.

A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium — it speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, helping equilibrium to be reached faster.

Key Fact

Le Chatelier’s principle: if conditions change, equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Catalysts speed up both reactions equally — they do not change the equilibrium position.

The Haber process manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen:

$$N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3$$

The forward reaction is exothermic. Conditions used: temperature of about 450°C, pressure of about 200 atmospheres, and an iron catalyst. The temperature is a compromise — lower temperature would give a higher yield but the rate would be too slow. The iron catalyst speeds up the reaction without changing the yield.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Crude Oil, Hydrocarbons and Cracking
chemistry-paper-2.description: How crude oil is separated by fractional distillation, alkane properties, and cracking.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
Crude Oil and Hydrocarbons

Crude oil is a finite resource formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient marine organisms. It is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons (molecules containing only hydrogen and carbon atoms).

The hydrocarbons in crude oil are separated by fractional distillation. The crude oil is heated until most of it evaporates. The vapours rise up a tall column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top. Different fractions condense at different heights depending on their boiling points: smaller molecules condense near the top (low boiling point) and larger molecules condense near the bottom (high boiling point).

Key Fact

Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation. Smaller hydrocarbons have lower boiling points, are less viscous, more flammable, and are collected near the top of the column. Larger hydrocarbons have higher boiling points and are collected near the bottom.

Alkanes

Most hydrocarbons in crude oil are alkanes. They have the general formula \(C_nH_{2n+2}\). The first four are:

  • Methane: \(CH_4\)
  • Ethane: \(C_2H_6\)
  • Propane: \(C_3H_8\)
  • Butane: \(C_4H_{10}\)

As the carbon chain gets longer: boiling point increases, viscosity increases (thicker), and flammability decreases (harder to ignite). These trends are due to stronger intermolecular forces between the larger molecules.

Hydrocarbons are used as fuels because they release energy when burned (combustion). Complete combustion (plenty of oxygen) produces carbon dioxide and water:

$$CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O$$

Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) produces carbon monoxide (toxic) and/or carbon (soot), as well as water. Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it is colourless, odourless, and binds to haemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport.

Cracking

Cracking is the process of breaking down long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful molecules. There is more demand for shorter-chain hydrocarbons (fuels like petrol) than for longer-chain ones. Cracking also produces alkenes, which are used to make polymers and other chemicals.

Key Fact

Cracking: long alkane → shorter alkane + alkene. Methods: catalytic cracking (hot catalyst) or steam cracking (high temperature + steam). Alkenes have a C=C double bond and are used to make polymers.

Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond (\(C=C\)) and have the general formula \(C_nH_{2n}\). They are described as unsaturated. You can test for the presence of a \(C=C\) double bond using bromine water: it turns from orange to colourless with an alkene (the bromine adds across the double bond). Alkanes do not decolourise bromine water because they are saturated (no double bonds).

chemistry-paper-2.title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests
chemistry-paper-2.description: How chemists test for purity, use chromatography, and identify common gases.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
Pure Substances and Mixtures

In chemistry, a pure substance consists of a single element or compound. It has a sharp, fixed melting point and boiling point. A mixture contains two or more substances not chemically combined. Mixtures melt over a range of temperatures rather than at a sharp point.

Key Fact

A pure substance has a sharp, specific melting point. An impure substance / mixture melts over a range of temperatures. You can test purity by checking the melting point against the known value.

Chromatography

Chromatography is used to separate and identify substances in a mixture. In paper chromatography, a spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil line on chromatography paper. The paper is placed in a solvent. As the solvent moves up the paper, it carries the dissolved substances with it. Different substances travel different distances depending on their solubility.

The R\(_f\) value is calculated as:

$$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent}}$$

Each substance has a unique \(R_f\) value in a given solvent. A pure substance produces a single spot; a mixture produces multiple spots.

You can identify substances by comparing their \(R_f\) values with known reference values, or by running known substances alongside the unknown on the same chromatogram. If a spot in the unknown lines up exactly with a spot from a known substance, they are the same compound.

Tests for Common Gases

You need to know the tests for four gases:

Key Fact

Gas tests: Hydrogen — squeaky pop with a lighted splint. Oxygen — relights a glowing splint. Carbon dioxide — turns limewater milky/cloudy. Chlorine — bleaches damp litmus paper white.

A formulation is a mixture designed as a useful product, where each component is present in a measured quantity to give it specific properties. Examples include medicines (active ingredient + binder + coating), paints (pigment + solvent + binder), and alloys (metals mixed in specific ratios for desired properties).

Formulations are found everywhere in everyday life. Each ingredient has a specific purpose, and changing the proportions changes the properties of the product.

chemistry-paper-2.title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect
chemistry-paper-2.description: How the atmosphere evolved over billions of years and how greenhouse gases cause climate change.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
The Early Atmosphere

For the first billion years, the Earth’s atmosphere was very different from today. Scientists believe it was mainly carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen — similar to the atmospheres of Venus and Mars today. There was also water vapour, nitrogen and small amounts of methane and ammonia. This early atmosphere was produced by volcanic activity.

The water vapour condensed as the Earth cooled, forming the oceans. Over billions of years, the atmosphere changed dramatically:

Step 1: The first simple organisms (algae and photosynthetic bacteria) evolved in the oceans. They used \(CO_2\) for photosynthesis and released \(O_2\), gradually increasing the oxygen level in the atmosphere.

Step 2: \(CO_2\) was also removed by dissolving in the oceans, where it formed carbonates in sedimentary rocks and the shells/skeletons of marine organisms.

Step 3: As \(O_2\) levels increased, more complex life evolved. The ozone layer (\(O_3\)) formed, shielding life from UV radiation.

Key Fact

Today’s atmosphere: approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus small amounts of other gases (argon, water vapour). This has been roughly stable for 200 million years.

The Greenhouse Effect

Greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) absorb heat radiation (infrared) from the Earth’s surface and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards Earth. This natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough to support life.

However, human activities are increasing the concentrations of greenhouse gases:

  • Carbon dioxide — burning fossil fuels, deforestation.
  • Methane — agriculture (cattle farming, rice paddies), landfill sites.

This enhanced greenhouse effect is causing global warming — an increase in global average temperatures. The consequences include: sea level rise (thermal expansion and melting ice), more extreme weather events, changes to ecosystems and species distribution, and impacts on agriculture.

Key Fact

Human activities increase \(CO_2\) (fossil fuels, deforestation) and \(CH_4\) (farming, landfill). Enhanced greenhouse effect → global warming → rising sea levels, extreme weather, habitat loss.

A carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gases released over the life cycle of a product or activity. It can be reduced by: using renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, carbon capture and storage, reducing meat consumption, and reducing travel.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Atmospheric Pollutants and Their Effects
chemistry-paper-2.description: How burning fuels produces pollutants, and their effects on health and the environment.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
Pollutants from Fuels

When fossil fuels are burned, several pollutant gases can be released into the atmosphere. The type and amount of pollutant depends on the fuel and the conditions of combustion.

The main pollutants are:

  • Carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)) — produced by complete combustion of any hydrocarbon. A greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming.
  • Carbon monoxide (\(CO\)) — produced by incomplete combustion. A toxic, colourless, odourless gas that binds to haemoglobin in the blood, preventing it from carrying oxygen. Can cause death.
  • Soot / particulates (carbon particles) — also from incomplete combustion. Cause respiratory problems, make buildings dirty, and contribute to global dimming (blocking sunlight).
  • Sulfur dioxide (\(SO_2\)) — produced when fuels containing sulfur impurities are burned. Causes acid rain, which damages buildings (corrodes limestone/marble), kills trees and acidifies lakes.
  • Nitrogen oxides (\(NO_x\)) — formed when nitrogen and oxygen react at the high temperatures inside car engines. Also cause acid rain and respiratory problems.
Key Fact

Fossil fuel pollutants: \(CO_2\) (greenhouse gas), CO (toxic), soot (respiratory problems), \(SO_2\) (acid rain from sulfur impurities), \(NO_x\) (acid rain from high temperature reaction of \(N_2\) and \(O_2\)).

Reducing Pollution

Catalytic converters in car exhausts convert toxic carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into less harmful gases:

$$2CO + 2NO \rightarrow 2CO_2 + N_2$$

Flue gas desulfurisation removes \(SO_2\) from power station emissions by reacting it with calcium oxide or calcium carbonate, producing calcium sulfate (which can be used to make plaster).

Key Fact

Solutions: catalytic converters reduce CO and \(NO_x\), flue gas desulfurisation removes \(SO_2\). Using low-sulfur fuels, renewable energy, and electric vehicles also reduces pollution.

Air pollution is a global issue. Pollutants can travel long distances in the atmosphere, meaning emissions in one country can cause acid rain in another. International agreements (such as the Paris Agreement) aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Developing countries face challenges balancing economic growth with pollution reduction.

Alternative approaches to reducing pollution include: switching to renewable energy sources (wind, solar, hydroelectric), using electric or hydrogen-powered vehicles, improving fuel efficiency, and developing carbon capture and storage technologies.

chemistry-paper-2.title: Using Earth's Resources and Sustainability
chemistry-paper-2.description: How we use natural resources, potable water treatment, and sustainable development.
chemistry-paper-2.content_html:
Natural Resources and Products

Humans use the Earth’s natural resources to provide warmth, shelter, food, and transport. Some resources are finite (non-renewable) — they will eventually run out (e.g. fossil fuels, metal ores). Others are renewable — they can be replaced (e.g. timber, cotton).

Sustainable development means meeting the needs of today’s population without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs. Chemistry plays a vital role in sustainable development by finding alternatives to finite resources and reducing waste.

Key Fact

Sustainable development: meet today’s needs without compromising the future. Strategies include using renewable resources, recycling, reducing waste, and developing new materials (e.g. bioplastics).

Potable Water

Potable water is water that is safe to drink. It is not the same as pure water — it contains low levels of dissolved substances. In the UK, potable water is produced from fresh water (rivers, reservoirs) by:

  1. Filtration — passing through filter beds to remove large debris, gravel and sand.
  2. Sedimentation — allowing fine particles to settle out.
  3. Sterilisation — adding chlorine, or using UV light or ozone to kill bacteria and make water safe.

In areas with limited fresh water, sea water can be made potable by desalination. Methods include distillation (boiling the water and condensing the steam) and reverse osmosis (forcing water through a membrane that blocks salt). Both methods require significant energy, making them expensive.

Key Fact

UK potable water: fresh water → filtration → sedimentation → sterilisation (chlorine/UV/ozone). Desalination converts sea water but requires a lot of energy. Potable ≠ pure — it still contains some dissolved substances.

Waste Water Treatment

Waste water (sewage and industrial water) must be treated before release into the environment. The process includes:

Screening: large objects (rags, sticks) are removed by passing water through screens.

Sedimentation: solids settle out as sludge. The liquid effluent is separated.

Biological treatment: aerobic bacteria break down organic matter in the effluent. The sludge is also digested anaerobically by bacteria, producing biogas (methane) which can be used as fuel.

Final treatment: the cleaned water is tested and released back into rivers or the sea.

Life Cycle Assessments and Recycling

A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product at every stage: extracting raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, and disposal (landfill, recycling, or incineration). LCAs help companies make products more sustainable.

Reducing, reusing and recycling materials conserves finite resources, reduces energy consumption, and decreases the amount of waste going to landfill. However, recycling has its own costs (collection, sorting, processing energy) and LCAs can be subjective.

physics-paper-1.title: Energy Stores, Transfers and Power
physics-paper-1.description: How energy is stored, transferred between stores, and how to calculate power and work done.
physics-paper-1.content_html:
Energy Stores

Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between different energy stores. You need to know eight energy stores.

Key Fact

The eight energy stores are: kinetic, thermal, chemical, elastic potential, gravitational potential, electrostatic, magnetic, and nuclear.

Kinetic energy depends on the mass and speed of an object. The equation is:

$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$$

Where \(E_k\) is kinetic energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(v\) is speed in metres per second (m/s).

Gravitational potential energy depends on the mass, height, and gravitational field strength:

$$E_p = m g h$$

Where \(E_p\) is gravitational potential energy in joules, \(m\) is mass in kg, \(g\) is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth), and \(h\) is height in metres.

Elastic potential energy is stored when an object is stretched or compressed:

$$E_e = \frac{1}{2} k e^2$$

Where \(E_e\) is elastic potential energy in J, \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m, and \(e\) is the extension in metres. This only applies up to the limit of proportionality.

Energy Transfers

Energy moves between stores by four transfer pathways: mechanically (by forces), electrically (by currents), by heating, and by radiation (light, sound, or other waves).

When a ball is thrown upwards, energy transfers from the kinetic store to the gravitational potential store. At the top, the ball momentarily stops — all kinetic energy has become gravitational potential energy. As it falls, the transfer reverses.

Key Fact

The law of conservation of energy states that energy can be transferred usefully, stored, or dissipated — but cannot be created or destroyed. The total energy of a closed system always stays the same.

A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Calculate the speed just before it hits the ground (assume no air resistance).

Step 1: \(E_p = mgh = 2 \times 10 \times 5 = 100\) J

Step 2: Set \(E_k = E_p\), so \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 100\)

Step 3: \(v^2 = \frac{2 \times 100}{2} = 100\), so \(v = 10\) m/s

Work Done and Power

When a force moves an object, work done equals the energy transferred:

$$W = F s$$

Where \(W\) is work done in joules, \(F\) is force in newtons (N), and \(s\) is distance along the line of action of the force in metres.

Power is the rate of energy transfer:

$$P = \frac{E}{t} \quad \text{and} \quad P = \frac{W}{t}$$

Where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(E\) is energy transferred in joules, and \(t\) is time in seconds. One watt equals one joule per second.

If an object moves at constant speed, you can combine the equations: \(P = Fv\), where \(v\) is speed in m/s. This is useful for calculating the power output of engines or motors.

physics-paper-1.title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources
physics-paper-1.description: Why energy is always conserved, how to calculate efficiency, and the pros and cons of energy resources.
physics-paper-1.content_html:
Conservation of Energy

The law of conservation of energy states that energy can never be created or destroyed. In any energy transfer, the total energy before and after is always the same.

In a closed system, where nothing can enter or leave, the total energy stays constant. However, in most real-world situations energy is dissipated — it spreads out to the surroundings as thermal energy and becomes increasingly difficult to use.

Key Fact

Energy is never “lost” — when we say energy is wasted, we mean it has been transferred to less useful stores (usually thermal energy in the surroundings). The total energy in the system has not changed.

Efficiency

Efficiency tells you how good a device is at transferring energy to useful stores. It is calculated using:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}$$

Efficiency can also be calculated using power:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output power}}{\text{total input power}}$$

Efficiency is a ratio and has no units. It is always between 0 and 1. To express it as a percentage, multiply by 100. No device can ever be more than 100% efficient.

A motor uses 500 J of electrical energy and transfers 350 J to the kinetic store. Calculate the efficiency.

\(\text{efficiency} = \frac{350}{500} = 0.70\) or 70%

This means 70% of the input energy is usefully transferred. The remaining 30% (150 J) is dissipated as thermal energy due to friction and sound.

Key Fact

Ways to increase efficiency include reducing friction (lubrication, streamlining), using thermal insulation to reduce unwanted heating, and improving design to minimise energy dissipation.

Reducing Unwanted Energy Transfers

Thermal insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating. In a house, loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, and double glazing all reduce the amount of thermal energy lost to the surroundings.

Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts. This means less energy is wasted as heat in the thermal store, so more energy goes to the useful output.

The thicker the walls of a house, the slower the rate of thermal energy transfer. Cavity wall insulation traps air between the inner and outer walls. Since air is a poor conductor, this reduces energy transfer by conduction. Double glazing works on the same principle — a layer of gas between two panes of glass reduces conduction and convection.

Energy Resources

Energy resources can be classified as non-renewable or renewable.

Non-renewable resources include fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and nuclear fuel. These are finite — once used up, they cannot be replaced within a human timescale.

Renewable resources include solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, wave power, and biofuels. These are replenished naturally and will not run out.

Fossil fuels are reliable and produce large amounts of energy, but release carbon dioxide (contributing to climate change) and are running out. Nuclear power is reliable and produces no carbon dioxide during operation, but produces radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years.

Renewable resources produce no greenhouse gases during operation and will not run out. However, many are weather-dependent (solar, wind) or location-dependent (tidal, geothermal), and some have high initial costs or low power output compared to fossil fuels.

The UK is working towards generating more electricity from renewable sources to reduce carbon emissions and meet climate targets. However, a mix of energy resources is needed to ensure a reliable supply.

physics-paper-1.title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference
physics-paper-1.description: Covers electric current and charge, potential difference, resistance and ohm's law and more.
physics-paper-1.content_html:
Electric Current and Charge

Electric current is the flow of charge carriers through a conductor. In metals, these charge carriers are electrons that move through the wire when a voltage is applied.

Key Fact

Current is measured in amperes (A) and represents the amount of charge flowing past a point per second. The equation is \(I = \frac{Q}{t}\) where I is current, Q is charge in coulombs, and t is time in seconds.

Current is measured using an ammeter, which must be connected in series with the component you want to measure. This ensures all the current flows through the ammeter.

Potential Difference

Potential difference (also called voltage) is the driving force that pushes current around a circuit. It represents the energy transferred per coulomb of charge.

The equation for potential difference is:

$$V = \frac{W}{Q}$$

Where V is potential difference in volts, W is work done (energy transferred) in joules, and Q is charge in coulombs.

Potential difference is measured using a voltmeter. Unlike an ammeter, a voltmeter must be connected in parallel with the component. This allows it to measure the energy difference between the two points without affecting the current flow.

Think of potential difference like the height difference in a waterfall — the greater the height difference, the more energy each drop of water has when it reaches the bottom.

Resistance and Ohm's Law

Resistance opposes the flow of current in a circuit. Different materials and components have different resistances — metals have low resistance while insulators have very high resistance.

Key Fact

Ohm's Law states that \(V = I \times R\) where V is potential difference in volts, I is current in amperes, and R is resistance in ohms (Ω). This relationship only applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature.

You can rearrange Ohm's law to find any of the three quantities:

$$I = \frac{V}{R} \text{ and } R = \frac{V}{I}$$

The resistance of a wire depends on four factors: its length (longer = higher resistance), cross-sectional area (thicker = lower resistance), material (different metals have different resistivity), and temperature (higher temperature usually = higher resistance for metals).

Some components like filament bulbs are non-ohmic — their resistance changes with temperature, so they don't follow Ohm's law exactly.

Series Circuits

In a series circuit, components are connected end-to-end in a single loop. Current has only one path to follow.

Key Fact

In series circuits: current is the same everywhere (\(I_1 = I_2 = I_3\)), potential difference is shared between components (\(V_{total} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3\)), and total resistance equals the sum of individual resistances (\(R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\)).

If one component fails in a series circuit, the whole circuit stops working because the current path is broken. This is why old Christmas lights used to all go out when one bulb failed.

Parallel Circuits

In a parallel circuit, components are connected on separate branches. Current can follow multiple paths.

In parallel circuits, each component receives the full supply voltage. This is why household appliances are connected in parallel — each device gets the full 230V regardless of what other appliances are switched on.

In parallel circuits: potential difference is the same across each branch (\(V_1 = V_2 = V_3\)), total current equals the sum of branch currents (\(I_{total} = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\)), and total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance.

The formula for total resistance in parallel is: \(\frac{1}{R_{total}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}\)

Electrical Power

Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer in a circuit. It tells us how quickly electrical energy is being converted to other forms like heat, light or motion.

The basic power equation is:

$$P = V \times I$$

Where P is power in watts, V is potential difference in volts, and I is current in amperes. By combining this with Ohm's law, we get two more useful equations: \(P = I^2R\) and \(P = \frac{V^2}{R}\).

physics-paper-1.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
physics-paper-1.description: Rules for current, voltage and resistance in series and parallel circuits, plus I-V characteristics.
physics-paper-1.content_html:
Series Circuits

In a series circuit, all components are connected in a single loop. There is only one path for current to flow, so the current is the same at every point in the circuit.

Key Fact

In a series circuit: current is the same everywhere, potential differences add up to equal the supply voltage, and total resistance equals the sum of all individual resistances: \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\).

The potential difference is shared between components in series. The larger the resistance of a component, the greater its share of the total voltage. If two identical resistors are in series, each gets half the supply voltage.

A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor. Calculate the current and the voltage across each resistor.

Step 1: Total resistance \(R_{\text{total}} = 4 + 8 = 12 \; \Omega\)

Step 2: Current \(I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{12} = 1\) A (same throughout)

Step 3: \(V_1 = IR_1 = 1 \times 4 = 4\) V across the 4 Ω resistor

Step 4: \(V_2 = IR_2 = 1 \times 8 = 8\) V across the 8 Ω resistor

Check: \(4 + 8 = 12\) V, which equals the supply voltage.

Parallel Circuits

In a parallel circuit, components are connected on separate branches. Each branch provides a different path for the current to flow through.

Key Fact

In a parallel circuit: potential difference is the same across each branch, currents in the branches add up to give the total current from the supply, and total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance.

The total resistance of resistors in parallel is found using:

$$\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}$$

Adding more resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance, because there are more paths for the current. This means the total current from the battery increases.

Two resistors (6 Ω and 3 Ω) are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply. Calculate the current in each branch and the total current.

Branch 1: \(I_1 = \frac{V}{R_1} = \frac{12}{6} = 2\) A

Branch 2: \(I_2 = \frac{V}{R_2} = \frac{12}{3} = 4\) A

Total current: \(I_{\text{total}} = 2 + 4 = 6\) A

Investigating Components

You need to know the I-V characteristics of three components: fixed resistors (ohmic conductors), filament lamps, and diodes.

A fixed resistor gives a straight line through the origin on an I-V graph — current is directly proportional to voltage (Ohm’s law). A filament lamp gives a curve: as current increases, the wire heats up and resistance increases. A diode only conducts in one direction — it has very high resistance in reverse bias.

To investigate the I-V characteristics of a component, connect it in series with a variable resistor, ammeter, and power supply. Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the component. Vary the resistance using the variable resistor to change the current and voltage. Record pairs of I and V values, then swap the power supply connections to get negative values. Plot V on the x-axis and I on the y-axis.

Two other important components are the thermistor and the LDR (light-dependent resistor). A thermistor’s resistance drops as temperature rises, making it useful in temperature sensors. An LDR’s resistance drops as light intensity increases, making it useful in automatic lighting circuits.

physics-paper-1.title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid
physics-paper-1.description: Mains electricity, plug wiring and safety, power equations, and how the National Grid works.
physics-paper-1.content_html:
Domestic Electricity

The UK mains supply is alternating current (a.c.) at about 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz. This means the current changes direction 50 times per second. Batteries supply direct current (d.c.), which always flows in the same direction.

Key Fact

UK mains supply: alternating current (a.c.), approximately 230 V, frequency 50 Hz. Batteries supply direct current (d.c.).

The Three-Pin Plug

Most appliances connect to the mains via a three-pin plug. The three wires are:

Live wire (brown) — carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. It alternates between about +325 V and −325 V.

Neutral wire (blue) — completes the circuit. It is at, or close to, 0 V (earth potential).

Earth wire (green and yellow) — a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. It carries current to earth if a fault occurs, preventing electric shock.

The live wire is dangerous even when the switch is off, because it is still at 230 V relative to earth. If you touch it, a large potential difference exists between you and the ground, causing a current to flow through your body. This can cause serious injury or death. A switch is always connected in the live wire so that when it is off, no current can reach the appliance.

Key Fact

The fuse is connected in the live wire. If too much current flows (due to a fault), the fuse wire melts, breaking the circuit and preventing overheating or fire. A circuit breaker does the same job but can be reset instead of replaced.

Electrical Power and Energy Transfer

The power of an appliance tells you how much energy it transfers per second. Two equations link power to current and voltage:

$$P = IV$$

$$P = I^2 R$$

Where \(P\) is power in watts, \(I\) is current in amps, \(V\) is potential difference in volts, and \(R\) is resistance in ohms.

The energy transferred by an appliance depends on its power and how long it is used:

$$E = Pt$$

Where \(E\) is energy in joules, \(P\) is power in watts, and \(t\) is time in seconds. You can also use \(E = QV\), where \(Q\) is charge in coulombs.

A 2 kW kettle is used for 3 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred in joules and in kilowatt-hours.

In joules: \(E = Pt = 2000 \times 180 = 360{,}000\) J

In kWh: \(E = 2 \times \frac{3}{60} = 0.1\) kWh. If electricity costs 30p per kWh, the cost is \(0.1 \times 30 = 3\)p.

The National Grid

The National Grid is a network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to homes and businesses across the UK.

Electricity is transmitted at very high voltages (up to 400,000 V) and low currents. Since power lost as heat in the cables equals \(P = I^2 R\), reducing the current dramatically reduces the energy wasted.

Transformers change the voltage of an a.c. supply. A step-up transformer increases the voltage at the power station before transmission. A step-down transformer decreases the voltage near homes to a safe 230 V.

When voltage is increased, current decreases (assuming power stays the same: \(P = IV\)). This is why high-voltage transmission wastes less energy — the lower current means less heating in the cables.

physics-paper-1.title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State
physics-paper-1.description: Covers what is density?, the three states of matter, changes of state and more.
physics-paper-1.content_html:
What is Density?

Density is a measure of how much mass is packed into a given volume. Every material has its own characteristic density, which helps us identify different substances and predict whether they will float or sink.

Key Fact

Density is calculated using the equation: \(\text{density} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\) or \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\)

The unit for density is kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³), though you might also see grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³). To convert between these units, remember that 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

A block of wood has a mass of 800 g and a volume of 1000 cm³. Its density is:

$$\rho = \frac{800\text{ g}}{1000\text{ cm}^3} = 0.8\text{ g/cm}^3$$

Since this is less than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³), the wood will float.

The Three States of Matter

Matter exists in three main states: solid, liquid, and gas. The differences between these states depend on how the particles are arranged and how they move.

Key Fact

In solids, particles vibrate in fixed positions. In liquids, particles can slide past each other. In gases, particles move freely and rapidly in all directions.

Solids

In a solid, particles are packed closely together in a regular pattern. They are held in place by strong forces of attraction and can only vibrate about their fixed positions. This gives solids their definite shape and volume.

Liquids

In a liquid, particles are still close together but not in a regular arrangement. The forces between particles are weaker than in solids, allowing particles to move past each other. This means liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of their container.

Gases

In a gas, particles are far apart and move randomly at high speeds. The forces between particles are very weak. Gases have no definite shape or volume and will expand to fill any container.

Changes of State

When we heat or cool a substance, we can change its state. These changes are physical changes — the substance itself doesn’t change, only the arrangement and movement of its particles.

There are six possible changes of state:

  • Melting: solid → liquid (heating)
  • Freezing: liquid → solid (cooling)
  • Evaporation/Boiling: liquid → gas (heating)
  • Condensation: gas → liquid (cooling)
  • Sublimation: solid → gas (heating)
  • Deposition: gas → solid (cooling)

Temperature During Changes of State

During a change of state, the temperature remains constant even though we continue to supply energy. This is because the energy is being used to break or form bonds between particles rather than increase their kinetic energy.

Key Fact

The temperature at which a solid melts is called its melting point. The temperature at which a liquid boils is called its boiling point. These are characteristic properties of each substance.

Density Changes During State Changes

When a substance changes state, its density usually changes too. This happens because the particles become more or less tightly packed together, changing the volume while the mass stays the same.

Generally, solids are denser than liquids, which are denser than gases. However, there are important exceptions — ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats.

Water is unusual because its solid form (ice) is less dense than its liquid form. When water freezes, the molecules arrange themselves in a hexagonal crystal structure that takes up more space than the liquid arrangement.

Ice has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³ while liquid water has a density of 1.00 g/cm³. This 8% difference is enough to make ice float, which is crucial for life on Earth as it insulates water beneath from freezing completely.

Practical Applications

Understanding density and states of matter has many practical applications. Engineers use density to choose materials for different purposes — aircraft need low-density materials to reduce weight, while ship anchors need high-density materials to sink effectively.

In everyday life, we use changes of state constantly: cooking involves melting butter and boiling water, while refrigeration relies on condensation and evaporation cycles.

Exam Tip

When calculating density, always check your units carefully. Make sure mass is in kg and volume is in m³ for the standard SI unit of kg/m³. Remember that during changes of state, temperature stays constant — this is a common exam question.

Key Takeaways

  • Density equals mass divided by volume and is measured in kg/m³
  • The three states of matter differ in particle arrangement and movement
  • During changes of state, temperature remains constant while energy breaks or forms particle bonds

physics-paper-1.title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
physics-paper-1.description: Covers what is internal energy?, specific heat capacity, latent heat and changes of state and more.
physics-paper-1.content_html:
What is Internal Energy?

All matter is made up of particles that are constantly moving. The internal energy of a substance is the total energy stored by all the particles inside it. This energy comes from two sources:

  • The kinetic energy of particles moving around (vibrating, rotating, or moving freely)
  • The potential energy stored in the forces between particles
Key Fact

Internal energy increases when a substance is heated and decreases when it cools down. The internal energy determines both the temperature and the state of matter.

When you heat a substance, you transfer energy to it. This energy makes the particles move faster and can also change how they’re arranged. The amount of internal energy depends on the substance’s temperature, mass, and what material it’s made from.

Specific Heat Capacity

Different materials need different amounts of energy to heat up by the same amount. For example, water takes much more energy to heat up than copper. This property is called specific heat capacity.

The relationship between energy, mass, temperature change, and specific heat capacity is given by:

$$\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta T$$

Where:

  • \(\Delta E\) = change in thermal energy (J)
  • \(m\) = mass (kg)
  • \(c\) = specific heat capacity (J/kg°C)
  • \(\Delta T\) = temperature change (°C)
Key Fact

Water has a very high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C), which is why it’s good for heating systems and why coastal areas have milder temperatures than inland areas.

Materials with high specific heat capacity take more energy to heat up but also store more energy when hot. This makes them good thermal stores. Metals generally have lower specific heat capacities than water, which is why a metal spoon heats up quickly in hot soup.

Latent Heat and Changes of State

When you heat ice, something interesting happens. At first, the temperature rises as the ice warms up. But when it reaches 0°C, the temperature stops rising even though you’re still adding energy. Instead, the ice melts into water. This energy is called latent heat.

There are two main types of latent heat:

  • Latent heat of fusion — energy needed to melt a solid or freeze a liquid
  • Latent heat of vaporisation — energy needed to boil a liquid or condense a gas

The latent heat of vaporisation is always much larger than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance.

During a change of state, all the energy goes into breaking or forming bonds between particles rather than making them move faster. This is why the temperature stays constant during melting, boiling, condensing, or freezing.

The energy required for a change of state is calculated using: \(E = m \times L\), where \(E\) is energy (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(L\) is the specific latent heat (J/kg).

Particle Model Explanation

The particle model helps explain these energy changes. In a solid, particles vibrate in fixed positions with strong forces holding them together. When heated, particles vibrate more vigorously, increasing the temperature.

Solid to liquid (melting): Energy breaks some bonds between particles. They can now slide past each other but stay close together.

Liquid to gas (boiling): Energy completely overcomes forces between particles. They move freely and far apart.

Gas to liquid (condensing): Particles lose energy and forces pull them back together.

Liquid to solid (freezing): Particles lose more energy and lock into fixed positions.

This model explains why gases take up much more space than liquids or solids, and why different substances have different melting and boiling points — it depends on how strong the forces between their particles are.

physics-paper-1.title: Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Half-Life
physics-paper-1.description: How the atomic model developed, types of nuclear radiation, and calculating half-life.
physics-paper-1.content_html:
The Model of the Atom

Our understanding of atomic structure has developed over time. The first model was the solid sphere model proposed by Dalton in the early 1800s. He imagined atoms as tiny, indivisible balls.

In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model — a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons scattered throughout, like plums in a pudding.

Key Fact

In 1909, Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but some were deflected and a few bounced back. This proved the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons orbiting at a distance — the nuclear model.

Bohr refined the nuclear model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances in fixed energy levels (shells). Niels Bohr’s model explained why atoms emit and absorb specific frequencies of electromagnetic radiation.

Later, James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, completing our picture of the atom: a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in energy levels.

Radioactive Decay

Some atomic nuclei are radioactive — they are unstable and emit radiation to become more stable. This process is called radioactive decay and is random. You cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay.

Key Fact

There are three types of nuclear radiation: alpha (\(\alpha\)) particles, beta (\(\beta\)) particles, and gamma (\(\gamma\)) rays. Each has different properties, penetrating power, and ionising ability.

Alpha (\(\alpha\)) — two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus). Strongly ionising, stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air. The atomic number decreases by 2 and the mass number decreases by 4.

Beta (\(\beta\)) — a high-speed electron emitted when a neutron turns into a proton. Moderately ionising, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. The atomic number increases by 1, mass number stays the same.

Gamma (\(\gamma\)) — an electromagnetic wave with no mass or charge. Weakly ionising, only reduced significantly by several centimetres of lead or thick concrete. The atomic number and mass number are unchanged.

Half-Life

The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for half the unstable nuclei to decay, or for the count rate (activity) to fall to half its original value.

After one half-life, half the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives, a quarter remain. After three half-lives, one-eighth remain, and so on.

A sample has an activity of 800 Bq. After 30 minutes, the activity is 100 Bq. Calculate the half-life.

800 → 400 → 200 → 100 = three half-lives

Three half-lives = 30 minutes, so one half-life = \(\frac{30}{3} = 10\) minutes.

Uses and Hazards of Radiation

Nuclear radiation has useful applications: gamma rays are used in medical tracers and to sterilise equipment; beta radiation is used in thickness gauges; alpha sources are used in smoke detectors.

Contamination occurs when radioactive material gets onto or inside the body. This is more dangerous because the source stays close to cells. Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an outside source — once the source is removed, the exposure stops.

Precautions include: keeping radioactive sources in lead-lined containers, using tongs to handle sources, wearing protective clothing, and minimising exposure time.

physics-paper-2.title: Forces, Gravity and Resultant Forces
physics-paper-2.description: Types of forces, gravity and weight calculations, and how to find the resultant force.
physics-paper-2.content_html:
What Are Forces?

A force is a push or a pull that acts on an object. Forces are measured in newtons (N) and are vector quantities — they have both a magnitude (size) and a direction.

Forces can be contact forces or non-contact forces. Contact forces include friction, air resistance, tension, and normal contact force. Non-contact forces include gravitational, electrostatic, and magnetic forces.

Key Fact

A force is an interaction between two objects. When two objects interact, each exerts a force on the other — these are equal in size and opposite in direction (Newton’s third law).

Gravity and Weight

Gravity is a non-contact force that attracts any two objects with mass. The strength of gravity depends on the masses of the objects and the distance between them.

Weight is the force of gravity acting on an object. It depends on the mass and the gravitational field strength:

$$W = mg$$

Where \(W\) is weight in newtons, \(m\) is mass in kilograms, and \(g\) is gravitational field strength in N/kg. On Earth, \(g \approx 10\) N/kg. On the Moon, \(g \approx 1.6\) N/kg.

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. It is the same everywhere. Weight is a force and depends on the gravitational field strength at that location. An astronaut with a mass of 80 kg weighs 800 N on Earth (\(80 \times 10\)) but only 128 N on the Moon (\(80 \times 1.6\)).

Weight is measured using a Newton meter (spring balance). Mass is measured using a balance.

Resultant Forces

When multiple forces act on an object, they can be replaced by a single force that has the same effect. This is called the resultant force.

Key Fact

If forces act in the same direction, add them. If forces act in opposite directions, subtract the smaller from the larger. The resultant force acts in the direction of the larger force.

If the resultant force on an object is zero, the object is in equilibrium. This means it is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity. If the resultant force is not zero, the object will accelerate in the direction of the resultant force.

A free body diagram shows all the forces acting on a single object. Each force is drawn as an arrow starting from the object, with the length of the arrow representing the force’s magnitude and the direction showing which way it acts.

For example, a book on a table has two forces: weight acting downwards and the normal contact force acting upwards. If these are equal, the resultant force is zero and the book stays still.

When two forces do not act along the same line, you can find the resultant using a scale drawing. Draw the forces as arrows, tip-to-tail, to scale. The resultant is the arrow from the start of the first force to the end of the second. Measure its length and angle.

physics-paper-2.title: Work Done, Elasticity and Hooke's Law
physics-paper-2.description: Calculating work done, investigating springs with Hooke's law, and elastic potential energy.
physics-paper-2.content_html:
Work Done

When a force causes an object to move, energy is transferred. The amount of energy transferred is called the work done. Work done is calculated using:

$$W = F s$$

Where \(W\) is work done in joules (J), \(F\) is force in newtons (N), and \(s\) is the distance moved along the line of action of the force in metres (m).

Key Fact

One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre in the direction of the force. Work done equals energy transferred: \(W = E\).

If a force acts at right angles to the direction of motion, no work is done. For example, gravity does no work on a satellite in a circular orbit because the force is perpendicular to the direction of travel.

A box is pushed 8 m across a floor against a friction force of 25 N. Calculate the work done against friction.

\(W = Fs = 25 \times 8 = 200\) J

This 200 J is transferred to the thermal energy store of the box and floor — they warm up slightly.

Hooke’s Law

Hooke’s law states that the extension of an elastic object is directly proportional to the force applied, as long as the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.

$$F = k e$$

Where \(F\) is force in newtons, \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m, and \(e\) is the extension in metres.

Key Fact

A force-extension graph for a spring is a straight line through the origin up to the limit of proportionality. Beyond this point, the graph curves and the spring no longer returns to its original length when the force is removed — it has been permanently deformed.

Hang a spring from a clamp stand. Measure the original (natural) length. Add masses one at a time and record the new length each time. Calculate the extension by subtracting the original length from the stretched length.

Plot a force-extension graph. The gradient of the straight-line section gives the spring constant \(k\). Use a ruler with a pointer (set square) to reduce parallax error when measuring length.

Elastic Potential Energy

When a spring is stretched or compressed within its limit of proportionality, it stores elastic potential energy. This can be calculated using:

$$E_e = \frac{1}{2} k e^2$$

Where \(E_e\) is elastic potential energy in joules, \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m, and \(e\) is the extension in metres.

A spring with a spring constant of 40 N/m is stretched by 0.15 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored.

\(E_e = \frac{1}{2} k e^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 0.15^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 0.0225 = 0.45\) J

An object that returns to its original shape after the force is removed is called elastic. An object that is permanently deformed is said to have undergone inelastic deformation.

physics-paper-2.title: Speed, Velocity and Acceleration
physics-paper-2.description: Speed, velocity and acceleration equations, plus interpreting distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
physics-paper-2.content_html:
Speed and Distance

Speed is a scalar quantity — it tells you how fast something is moving but not the direction. The equation for speed is:

$$s = v t$$

Where \(s\) is distance in metres, \(v\) is speed in m/s, and \(t\) is time in seconds. This can be rearranged to \(v = \frac{s}{t}\).

Key Fact

Typical speeds: walking ~1.5 m/s, running ~3 m/s, cycling ~6 m/s, car in town ~13 m/s, car on motorway ~30 m/s, train ~55 m/s, aeroplane ~250 m/s, sound in air ~330 m/s.

Velocity

Velocity is a vector quantity. It has both magnitude (speed) and direction. An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because its direction is always changing.

The difference between speed and velocity matters in physics: two cars travelling at 30 m/s in opposite directions have the same speed but different velocities.

Acceleration

Acceleration is how quickly an object’s velocity changes. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{\Delta v}{t} = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

Where \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\), \(v\) is final velocity, \(u\) is initial velocity, and \(t\) is time in seconds. A negative acceleration means the object is decelerating (slowing down).

Key Fact

For uniform (constant) acceleration, use the equation: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\), where \(s\) is the distance travelled. This is particularly useful when time is not given in the question.

A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate the acceleration.

\(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{30 - 10}{5} = \frac{20}{5} = 4\) m/s\(^2\)

Distance-Time Graphs

A distance-time graph shows how far an object has travelled over time. The gradient (slope) of the line gives the speed.

A horizontal line means the object is stationary. A straight diagonal line means constant speed. A curve getting steeper means the object is accelerating. The steeper the line, the faster the object is moving.

To find the speed at a specific moment on a curved distance-time graph, draw a tangent to the curve at that point. Then calculate the gradient of the tangent: \(\text{speed} = \frac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}\).

Velocity-Time Graphs

A velocity-time graph shows how velocity changes over time. The gradient gives the acceleration. The area under the line gives the total distance travelled.

A horizontal line means constant velocity (no acceleration). A line sloping upwards means acceleration. A line sloping downwards means deceleration. The area under the graph can be found by splitting it into rectangles and triangles.

Use a dynamics trolley on a ramp with a light gate or ticker tape timer. Vary the force (by changing the mass on a pulley) while keeping the total mass constant. Measure the acceleration for each force. Plot a graph of force against acceleration — a straight line through the origin shows that \(F = ma\).

physics-paper-2.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
physics-paper-2.description: Newton's three laws of motion, inertia, F = ma calculations, and terminal velocity.
physics-paper-2.content_html:
Newton’s First Law

Newton’s first law states that an object will remain at rest or continue to move at a constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.

This means that if all forces on an object are balanced (resultant force = 0), the object will not change its motion. A stationary object stays still. A moving object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.

Key Fact

Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist a change in motion. The more mass an object has, the greater its inertia. This is why a heavy object is harder to push into motion or bring to a stop than a light one.

Newton’s Second Law

Newton’s second law states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass:

$$F = m a$$

Where \(F\) is the resultant force in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\).

This tells us three things: a larger force produces a greater acceleration; a larger mass requires a greater force for the same acceleration; and if the resultant force is zero, there is no acceleration.

A 1200 kg car has a driving force of 4800 N and friction of 1200 N. Calculate the acceleration.

Step 1: Resultant force = 4800 − 1200 = 3600 N

Step 2: \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{3600}{1200} = 3\) m/s\(^2\)

Newton’s Third Law

Newton’s third law states that whenever two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. These forces act on different objects and are always the same type of force.

Key Fact

Newton’s third law pairs always: act on two different objects, are the same size, act in opposite directions, and are the same type of force. For example, the Earth pulls you down with gravity, and you pull the Earth up with the same gravitational force.

Students often confuse balanced forces with Newton’s third law pairs. Balanced forces act on the same object (e.g. weight and normal force on a book). Newton’s third law pairs act on different objects (e.g. the book pushes the table down, the table pushes the book up).

Another misconception: “if the forces are equal and opposite, the object can’t move.” This is wrong because the two forces act on different objects. A rocket accelerates because the rocket pushes gas backwards and the gas pushes the rocket forwards — these act on different objects.

Terminal Velocity

When an object falls through a fluid (air or water), it initially accelerates due to gravity. As its speed increases, the drag force (air resistance) increases. Eventually, the drag force equals the weight and the resultant force becomes zero.

At this point, the object reaches terminal velocity — it continues to fall at a constant speed because the forces are balanced.

When a skydiver jumps, they accelerate because weight is greater than air resistance. As speed increases, air resistance increases, so acceleration decreases. At terminal velocity (~55 m/s), forces are balanced. When the parachute opens, air resistance suddenly increases above the weight, so the skydiver decelerates. A new, lower terminal velocity (~5 m/s) is reached.

physics-paper-2.title: Stopping Distances, Braking and Momentum
physics-paper-2.description: Covers what are stopping distances?, braking forces and energy, understanding momentum and more.
physics-paper-2.content_html:
What Are Stopping Distances?

When a vehicle needs to stop, it doesn't happen instantly. The stopping distance is made up of two parts: thinking distance and braking distance.

Key Fact

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

The thinking distance is how far the car travels while the driver reacts to a hazard. During this time, the vehicle continues at constant speed.

The braking distance is how far the car travels while the brakes are being applied and the vehicle is decelerating.

Several factors can increase thinking distance:

  • Tiredness or fatigue reduces reaction speed
  • Drugs and alcohol slow down the nervous system
  • Distractions like mobile phones delay reactions
  • Higher speeds mean more distance covered during reaction time

Braking Forces and Energy

When brakes are applied, friction between the brake pads and wheels creates a force that opposes motion. This braking force does work against the vehicle's kinetic energy.

The work done by braking forces transfers the vehicle's kinetic energy into heat energy at the brakes. We can calculate this using:

$$\text{Work done by brakes} = \text{Braking force} \times \text{Braking distance}$$

This work done equals the kinetic energy that was lost: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\)

Key Fact

Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed. Double the speed means four times the braking distance.

Braking distance increases when:

  • Vehicle speed is higher — kinetic energy increases with speed squared
  • Vehicle mass is greater — more kinetic energy to remove
  • Road conditions are poor — wet or icy roads reduce friction
  • Brake or tyre condition is poor — worn components reduce braking force

Understanding Momentum

Every moving object has momentum. Momentum is calculated using:

$$\text{momentum} = \text{mass} \times \text{velocity}$$

$$p = m \times v$$

Momentum is measured in kg⋅m/s and is a vector quantity — it has both size and direction.

In any collision or explosion, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after. This is the conservation of momentum.

For two objects colliding:

$$m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$$

Where \(u\) represents initial velocities and \(v\) represents final velocities.

Vehicle Safety Features

Modern vehicles use momentum principles to improve safety during collisions. The key is to increase the time over which momentum changes occur.

Using \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\), we can see that increasing the time (\(\Delta t\)) for a momentum change reduces the force experienced.

Key Fact

Safety features work by increasing collision time, which reduces the forces acting on passengers.

Examples of safety features include:

  • Crumple zones — designed to deform and extend collision time
  • Airbags — inflate to cushion impact and increase stopping time
